meta.blurb: Suffering follows a troubled mind, says an old verse, the way a cart wheel follows the ox. The Dhammapada gathers short sayings linked to the Buddha on anger, habit and peace, each one small enough to carry through your day.
meta.bible: The Dhammapada: a Buddhist collection of 423 short verses in 26 chapters, part of the Pali Canon (the Khuddaka Nikaya); the name is often translated as the path of the teaching. Buddha: the awakened teacher who lived in northern India more than two thousand years ago; tradition links the verses to his teaching. Pali: the ancient language of the verses. Dhamma: the teaching. Nibbana: the freedom of a mind at peace. Mara: the tempter who stands for everything that holds the heart in sleep. Arahant: the worthy one who has reached the end of the path. Brahmin: here a truly noble person, one who is noble by conduct, not by birth. Noble Eightfold Path and Four Noble Truths: the core of the teaching. Sangha: the community of monks. Gotama: the family name of the Buddha. Himalaya: the great mountain range of the north. The 26 chapters, in order, are Twin Verses, Heedfulness, Mind, Flowers, The Fool, The Wise, The Worthy, Thousands, Evil, Punishment, Old Age, The Self, The World, The Buddha, Happiness, Affection, Anger, Impurity, The Just, The Path, Miscellaneous, Hell, The Elephant, Craving, The Monk, The Brahmin. The retelling follows this order and gives each Dhammapada chapter several beats; the twenty chapters of ten beats are the book's own divisions and cut across the Dhammapada's. Stories that tradition links to verses, always introduced as tradition and never as fact: Cakkhupala, a blind monk who stepped on insects without meaning harm (first verse); Culapanthaka, a slow student who learned by patient effort (Heedfulness); Pandita, a young novice who learned to tame himself (The Wise); Kisa Gotami, a grieving mother who sought a cure and learned about death (Thousands); Visakha, a woman who grieved for her granddaughter (Affection); Angulimala, a feared bandit who gave up violence and became a monk (The World). The Buddha is said to have spoken the words about the house-builder at his awakening. Verses are numbered 1 to 423, and a few are mentioned by chapter only. Voice and tone: calm, kind, respectful and plain; verses are paraphrased and never copied; nothing is preached and no other tradition is compared or criticised; no gore; dark subjects such as death and suffering are treated factually and gently.

beats.scene: A monk reads a long palm-leaf manuscript by lamplight in a quiet hall
beats.summary: The Dhammapada is introduced as a collection of 423 verses in 26 chapters.

beats.scene: Villagers sit in a circle listening as a teacher recites a short verse
beats.summary: How to read the book: the verses are short, tradition adds a story to each, and this retelling follows the chapter order.

beats.scene: An ox pulls a heavy cart along a dusty road
beats.summary: Twin Verses: the mind comes first, and an angry mind brings suffering like a wheel following the ox.

beats.scene: A calm woman walks in bright sunlight with her long shadow beside her
beats.summary: Twin Verses: a kind mind brings happiness that follows like a shadow.

beats.scene: A blind monk walks slowly with a stick along a garden path
beats.summary: Twin Verses: the story of Cakkhupala, the blind monk who stepped on insects without meaning harm.

beats.scene: A man counts old grievances on his fingers, then opens his hand
beats.summary: Twin Verses: those who keep thinking of wrongs done to them never end their hatred.

beats.scene: Two neighbours at a fence, one holding out an open hand
beats.summary: Twin Verses: hatred is never ended by hatred, only by love.

beats.scene: A crowd argues loudly in a market while one old man watches quietly
beats.summary: Twin Verses: those who remember that everyone must die let their quarrels end.

beats.scene: Wind bends a thin tree while a rocky mountain stands untouched
beats.summary: Twin Verses: the careless are shaken like a weak tree in the wind, the self-controlled stand like a mountain.

beats.scene: A monk's plain yellow robe hangs folded on a wooden bench
beats.summary: Twin Verses: a robe is worthy only of one who is honest and self-controlled.

beats.scene: A man weighs a bag of husks and a bag of grain
beats.summary: Twin Verses: those who mistake the unimportant for the important never reach what matters.

beats.scene: Rain pours through a hole in an old thatched roof into a bare room
beats.summary: Twin Verses: passion enters an untrained mind like rain through a badly thatched roof.

beats.scene: A woman smiles over a harvest she grew while a man hides his face
beats.summary: Twin Verses: the wrongdoer grieves in this life and the next, the doer of good rejoices.

beats.scene: A cowherd counts another man's cattle at the edge of a field
beats.summary: Twin Verses: reciting many scriptures without practising is like counting another's cows.

beats.scene: A traveller wakes early and lights a lamp beside a door
beats.summary: Heedfulness: care leads to life at its fullest, carelessness to a kind of death.

beats.scene: A merchant checks every strap on his loaded mule at dawn
beats.summary: Heedfulness: the energetic, mindful, honest and considerate person's good name grows.

beats.scene: A small green island stands firm in a wide flooded river
beats.summary: Heedfulness: by effort and self-control the wise make an island no flood can cover.

beats.scene: A boy sits on a step rubbing a clean white cloth
beats.summary: Heedfulness: the story of Culapanthaka, the slow student who learned by patient effort.

beats.scene: A woman locks a strongbox while a gambler laughs loudly beyond a door
beats.summary: Heedfulness: fools give themselves to carelessness, the wise guard care as their best treasure.

beats.scene: A woman on a high tower looks down on a crowded plain
beats.summary: Heedfulness: the wise climb above carelessness and look calmly on those who still struggle.

beats.scene: A swift horse gallops ahead of a tired pony at dawn
beats.summary: Heedfulness: awake among sleepers, the wise move on like a fast horse leaving a weak one behind.

beats.scene: A small fire burns a dry heap of brush at a field's edge
beats.summary: Heedfulness: one who delights in care burns through every bond like a fire.

beats.scene: A craftsman carefully straightens a wooden arrow shaft in his hands
beats.summary: Mind: the wise straighten the trembling mind as a maker of arrows straightens a shaft.

beats.scene: A silver fish thrashes on dry sand beside a river
beats.summary: Mind: the mind struggles like a fish thrown on dry land when it is pulled from its old habits.

beats.scene: A runaway horse slows to a gentle walk beside its rider
beats.summary: Mind: a mind that has been tamed brings happiness.

beats.scene: A lantern burns steadily in a dark cave deep in the hills
beats.summary: Mind: the mind is subtle and wanders far, and those who guard it find peace.

beats.scene: A boy chases a butterfly across a field and then sits still
beats.summary: Mind: an unsteady mind cannot gain wisdom, a mind free from craving has no fear.

beats.scene: A guard on a small stone city wall holds a clay jar
beats.summary: Mind: treat the body as a fragile jar and the mind as a guarded city.

beats.scene: A fallen tree trunk lies unmoving beside a forest path
beats.summary: Mind: soon this body will lie on the ground like a useless log.

beats.scene: A mother and father embrace their grown child at the door of a house
beats.summary: Mind: a wrongly directed mind harms us more than an enemy, a well-directed one helps more than a parent.

beats.scene: A gardener picks flowers carefully in a field of blossoms
beats.summary: Flowers: a learner picks out the well-taught lesson as a skilled gardener picks flowers.

beats.scene: White foam on a river dissolves as a flood rolls toward a sleeping village
beats.summary: Flowers: the body is like foam, and death carries off the distracted like a flood a sleeping village.

beats.scene: A bee drinks nectar from a blossom without bending a single petal
beats.summary: Flowers: a bee takes nectar without harming the flower, and the sage passes through a village as gently.

beats.scene: A man reads a notice board while his own garden is overgrown with weeds
beats.summary: Flowers: look at your own deeds, not at the faults of others.

beats.scene: A bright paper flower without any scent lies beside a real rose
beats.summary: Flowers: fine words without action are like beautiful flowers without scent.

beats.scene: A woman strings many coloured flowers into a long garland
beats.summary: Flowers: as many garlands can be made from a heap of flowers, so much good can be done in one life.

beats.scene: Wind carries petals and scent from a garden along a road toward the town
beats.summary: Flowers: the scent of flowers cannot go against the wind, but the fragrance of the good spreads everywhere.

beats.scene: A pink lotus blooms on a rubbish heap beside a busy highway
beats.summary: Flowers: a lotus grows fragrant on a rubbish heap, so a wise person shines among the heedless.

beats.scene: A tired traveller lies awake at night, staring at a dark ceiling
beats.summary: The Fool: the night is long to the sleepless and the road to the weary, and life to those who ignore the truth.

beats.scene: A lone traveller walks a long road at sunset with no companion
beats.summary: The Fool: if no better or equal companion can be found, go on alone rather than with a fool.

beats.scene: A rich merchant counts coins at night beside a sleeping child
beats.summary: The Fool: the fool frets over my children and my wealth, though even the self cannot be held for ever.

beats.scene: A man laughs gently at himself after dropping his books in the street
beats.summary: The Fool: a fool who knows he is a fool is wise to that extent, one who thinks he is wise is the real fool.

beats.scene: A wooden spoon rests in a bowl of hot soup on a kitchen table
beats.summary: The Fool: a fool beside the wise understands nothing, as a spoon cannot taste soup, while the wise learn quickly.

beats.scene: A man sits with his face in his hands beside a broken vase
beats.summary: The Fool: a deed that brings regret and tears is poorly done, one that brings joy without regret is well done.

beats.scene: A jar of honey and a glowing ember sit side by side
beats.summary: The Fool: wrongdoing tastes like honey until it ripens, then it burns like a hidden ember.

beats.scene: A proud man in fine clothes takes the best seat at a crowded feast
beats.summary: The Fool: the fool wants fame, rank and first place, and that wish ruins him.

beats.scene: Two roads fork at a signpost in a green valley
beats.summary: The Fool: one road leads to gain and another to nibbana, so do not chase honour.

beats.scene: A woman points out a stain on a man's coat and he thanks her
beats.summary: The Wise: one who points out our faults is like one who shows hidden treasure.

beats.scene: Two friends share a bench near a tidy, candlelit house
beats.summary: The Wise: keep good friends and avoid bad ones.

beats.scene: A man drinks clear water from his cupped hand beside a mountain stream
beats.summary: The Wise: those who drink the teaching live happily with a clear mind.

beats.scene: A young novice stands beside a craftsman who straightens an arrow
beats.summary: The Wise: the story of Pandita, a young novice; the wise tame themselves as fletchers straighten arrows.

beats.scene: A great grey rock stands firm as wind bends the trees
beats.summary: The Wise: like a solid rock in the wind, the wise are not moved by praise or blame.

beats.scene: A deep clear mountain lake lies perfectly still in the morning light
beats.summary: The Wise: after hearing the teachings, the wise become calm like a clear, deep lake.

beats.scene: A woman lets a gift go with a calm face while others cry out
beats.summary: The Wise: the good let go, and the wise show neither elation nor despair at joy or sorrow.

beats.scene: A crowd runs along a river bank while a few cross by boat
beats.summary: The Wise: few cross to the far shore, and most run up and down the bank.

beats.scene: A person walks away from a dark valley toward a bright hilltop
beats.summary: The Wise: the wise leave the dark way for the bright and become luminous.

beats.scene: A smiling monk stands at the end of a mountain road
beats.summary: The Worthy: for one who has finished the journey there is no sorrow and no fever of the heart.

beats.scene: A flock of swans lifts off a lake and leaves the shore behind
beats.summary: The Worthy: like swans leaving a lake, the mindful do not cling to any home.

beats.scene: A single bird flies across a wide empty sky leaving no track
beats.summary: The Worthy: the path of the free is as hard to trace as a bird's path in the sky.

beats.scene: A charioteer holds the reins of a calm, well-matched pair of horses
beats.summary: The Worthy: even the gods admire one whose senses are tamed like well-trained horses.

beats.scene: A calm monk stands still like a pillar as children run past
beats.summary: The Worthy: such a person is patient like the earth, steady like a pillar and clear like a lake without mud.

beats.scene: A quiet forest clearing where a lone monk walks happily at dawn
beats.summary: The Worthy: calm in thought, word and deed, and wherever the worthy live the place is delightful.

beats.scene: An old teacher whispers one quiet word to a student in a crowded hall
beats.summary: Thousands: one word of meaning that brings peace is better than a thousand empty words.

beats.scene: A warrior sits alone with closed eyes and his sword laid on the ground
beats.summary: Thousands: the one who conquers himself is a greater conqueror than one who defeats a thousand men.

beats.scene: A woman bows to an elder in a plain room beside unused costly offerings
beats.summary: Thousands: one moment of respect for a good person is worth more than a year of costly offerings.

beats.scene: A young man helps an elderly neighbour up a flight of steps
beats.summary: Thousands: for one who honours elders, four things grow: life, beauty, happiness and strength.

beats.scene: A candle burns brightly beside a calendar of a hundred empty pages
beats.summary: Thousands: one day lived with virtue and thought is better than a hundred years of carelessness.

beats.scene: A woman rises at dawn and sets about a hard task with energy
beats.summary: Thousands: one day of firm effort is better than a hundred years of laziness.

beats.scene: Waves rise and fall on a river under a still, watching sky
beats.summary: Thousands: one day of seeing how things arise and pass away beats a hundred years of not seeing.

beats.scene: A young mother stands at a doorway holding a small mustard seed
beats.summary: Thousands: the story of Kisa Gotami, who sought a cure for her grief and learned about death.

beats.scene: A book lies open on a table in morning light
beats.summary: Thousands: one day of seeing the highest teaching is better than a hundred years without it.

beats.scene: A girl hurries to carry an old woman's heavy basket
beats.summary: Evil: hurry to do good and keep the mind from evil, or the mind will start to enjoy wrongdoing.

beats.scene: A boy turns away from a shiny coin on a market stall
beats.summary: Evil: if you do wrong, do not do it again and again, and if you do good, do it again and again.

beats.scene: A farmer looks at ripening fruit on a branch beside a sour one
beats.summary: Evil: the wrongdoer may seem to prosper until the deed ripens, and the good may seem to suffer until the good ripens.

beats.scene: A water jar slowly fills under a roof as drops fall one by one
beats.summary: Evil: a jar is filled drop by drop, and so is a person with good or with evil.

beats.scene: A merchant with a small escort and rich cargo avoids a dangerous road
beats.summary: Evil: avoid evil as a rich merchant avoids a dangerous road, or as one who loves life avoids poison.

beats.scene: A person throws a handful of dust into a strong wind
beats.summary: Evil: harm done to the innocent comes back like fine dust thrown against the wind.

beats.scene: A man looks over sky, sea and a cave but finds nowhere to hide
beats.summary: Evil: nowhere in sky, sea or mountain can one hide from one's own deeds.

beats.scene: Children stop a fight in a schoolyard and hold hands
beats.summary: Punishment: all tremble at violence and fear death, so see yourself in others and harm no one.

beats.scene: A boy gently stops an older boy from throwing a stone at a bird
beats.summary: Punishment: those who seek happiness by harming others will not find it, and those who harm no one will.

beats.scene: A woman answers a shouting neighbour with silence while an echo rolls back
beats.summary: Punishment: do not speak harshly, for those you speak to will answer back.

beats.scene: A cracked brass gong hangs silent in a quiet temple courtyard
beats.summary: Punishment: if you can be still as a cracked gong, you have reached peace and no quarrel remains.

beats.scene: A cowherd drives a herd of cows with a stick toward a pasture
beats.summary: Punishment: as a cowherd drives cows, so old age and death drive our lives forward.

beats.scene: A man covered in ashes sits beside a plainly dressed calm woman
beats.summary: Punishment: outward show does not purify, but a calm and kind heart does.

beats.scene: A fine horse lifts its head at the touch of a whip
beats.summary: Punishment: be like a good horse that responds to the lightest touch, with faith, effort and thought.

beats.scene: Lanterns glow on a festival street while night presses in
beats.summary: Old Age: why laugh and play when the world burns with wants, and why not look for a light?

beats.scene: A painted doll with a tiny crack sits in a window
beats.summary: Old Age: look at this decorated body, so fragile and always changing.

beats.scene: A weathered house of bare beams stands on a dark hill
beats.summary: Old Age: the body is like a house with bones for its frame, and in it live ageing, death, pride and deceit.

beats.scene: An old royal chariot, worn and faded, stands in a quiet courtyard
beats.summary: Old Age: even royal chariots wear out and the body grows old, but the teaching of the good does not age.

beats.scene: An old ox stands in a field, heavy and slow, chewing grass
beats.summary: Old Age: a person of little learning grows old like an ox, as the body grows and wisdom does not.

beats.scene: A builder looks up at a bare wooden frame under the stars
beats.summary: Old Age: tradition says the Buddha spoke of the house-builder, craving, at his awakening and promised it would build no more.

beats.scene: An old heron stands beside a pond with no fish at dusk
beats.summary: Old Age: those who never used their youth well pine like old herons beside a pond with no fish.

beats.scene: A woman sits by a lamp keeping watch in the dark night
beats.summary: The Self: if you hold yourself dear, guard yourself well and first practise what you teach.

beats.scene: A gardener prunes his own tree, then helps a neighbour with a hedge
beats.summary: The Self: do yourself as you teach others, for taming the self is the hardest task.

beats.scene: A traveller reaches a safe stone house at the top of a long climb
beats.summary: The Self: you are your own refuge, and a well-trained self is a refuge hard to find.

beats.scene: A creeper strangles a tall sala tree in a forest
beats.summary: The Self: harm done by oneself crushes the fool, as a creeper strangles a tree.

beats.scene: A man washes his own face and hands in a clear stream at dawn
beats.summary: The Self: we do wrong by ourselves and are made pure by ourselves, and no one can purify another.

beats.scene: A woman helps a friend while her own notebook of goals lies open
beats.summary: The Self: do not lose sight of your own real good, however much you do for others.

beats.scene: A sleeper wakes at dawn and rises from bed as light fills the window
beats.summary: The World: rise, do not be careless, and follow the good path, which brings happiness.

beats.scene: A soap bubble floats up and shimmers above a sunlit pond
beats.summary: The World: look upon the world as a bubble or a mirage, and as a painted royal chariot that fools sink into.

beats.scene: A former robber kneels before a calm teacher on a forest road
beats.summary: The World: the story of Angulimala, and how one careless before and careful later lights the world like the moon freed from a cloud.

beats.scene: A crowd stumbles around a dim hall while a few look toward a window
beats.summary: The World: this world is blind and few see clearly, and few escape like birds from a net.

beats.scene: Swans fly in a long line across a golden evening sky
beats.summary: The World: swans fly along the path of the sun, and the wise rise above the world after conquering Mara.

beats.scene: A miser's locked chest stands beside a woman handing out bread
beats.summary: The World: a liar who scoffs at everything can do any wrong, and the wise delight in giving.

beats.scene: A king on his throne looks toward a distant mountain and a hut
beats.summary: The World: better than ruling the whole earth is the first step on the path to freedom.

beats.scene: Footprints cross wet sand and then vanish at a rocky shore
beats.summary: The Buddha: whose victory cannot be undone and whom no craving follows, by what track would you lead such a one?

beats.scene: Monks meditate calmly under a great banyan tree at dusk
beats.summary: The Buddha: the wise delight in the peace of quiet meditation, and even the gods hold dear the awake and mindful.

beats.scene: A hiker stands on a mountain top at dawn, amazed at the view
beats.summary: The Buddha: it is hard to be born human, to live, to hear the true teaching and for a Buddha to arise.

beats.scene: Three simple lines of text are carved on a stone beside a monastery gate
beats.summary: The Buddha: avoid all evil, do good and purify the mind, with harmlessness, restraint, moderation and meditation.

beats.scene: A man stands quietly with his arms at his sides as someone shouts
beats.summary: The Buddha: patience is the highest discipline, and one who harms others is no true monk.

beats.scene: A shower of gold coins falls onto an empty marketplace
beats.summary: The Buddha: not even a rain of gold coins satisfies desire, and the disciple delights in the end of craving.

beats.scene: A frightened family prays at a stone shrine and a huge old tree
beats.summary: The Buddha: fear sends people to hills, forests and trees for refuge, but the safe refuge is the teaching and the four truths.

beats.scene: A rare white lotus opens in a bright morning garden
beats.summary: The Buddha: a Buddha is hard to find, and blessed are his birth, the teaching and the harmony of the community.

beats.scene: A man bows deeply to an elderly teacher in a quiet room
beats.summary: The Buddha: honour those worthy of honour, for the merit cannot be measured.

beats.scene: A village of neighbours shares a meal peacefully at one long table
beats.summary: Happiness: let us live happily without hate, without sickness and without worry, even among those who hate, are sick or worry.

beats.scene: Travellers with only small bundles laugh together around a fire
beats.summary: Happiness: let us live happily without possessions, feeding on joy.

beats.scene: Two chess players shake hands over a finished game
beats.summary: Happiness: victory breeds hatred, and the peaceful give up both victory and defeat.

beats.scene: A hungry child eats bread beside a flickering hearth
beats.summary: Happiness: no fire like lust, no crime like hatred, hunger is the worst illness and nibbana the highest happiness.

beats.scene: A farmer rests with bread and water in a quiet field and smiles
beats.summary: Happiness: health is the greatest gift, contentment the greatest wealth, trust the best kinsman.

beats.scene: A person sits alone by a calm lake, sipping a cup of spring water
beats.summary: Happiness: one who has tasted solitude and peace is free from fear and evil and drinks deep joy.

beats.scene: The moon moves among the stars above a group of friends on a roof
beats.summary: Happiness: it is good to see the noble and to live with them, so follow the wise as the moon follows the stars.

beats.scene: A woman looks toward an empty chair at the end of a table
beats.summary: Affection: it is painful not to see those we love and painful to see those we dislike.

beats.scene: A child lets go of a kite string and watches the kite rise calmly
beats.summary: Affection: parting from the dear is painful, and those who hold nothing too tightly have no bonds.

beats.scene: A man packs a small bag and looks back at a lamp-lit window
beats.summary: Affection: from affection come grief and fear, and one free from clinging has none.

beats.scene: A grandmother sits quietly beside a small empty bed
beats.summary: Affection: the story of Visakha, whose grief for her granddaughter taught her about affection.

beats.scene: A neighbour is welcomed warmly into a busy home
beats.summary: Affection: people hold dear one who has virtue and insight, speaks truly and does their duty.

beats.scene: A traveller returns home at dusk as friends run out to greet him
beats.summary: Affection: as friends welcome back a traveller, good deeds welcome one who has done good.

beats.scene: A man opens his clenched fists and sets down a heavy stone
beats.summary: Anger: abandon anger and give up pride, for no suffering falls on one who clings to nothing as mine.

beats.scene: A charioteer pulls firmly on the reins to stop a galloping team
beats.summary: Anger: one who checks rising anger like a runaway chariot is a true charioteer.

beats.scene: A woman answers an angry shouting man with a gentle smile and a gift
beats.summary: Anger: conquer anger by calm, evil by good, the miser by giving and the liar by truth.

beats.scene: A person gives half a loaf to a stranger in a village lane
beats.summary: Anger: speak the truth, do not yield to anger, and give even if you have little.

beats.scene: A silent man, a chatty man and a calm man each draw frowns
beats.summary: Anger: everyone is blamed, the silent, the talkative and the moderate, and no one is wholly blamed or wholly praised.

beats.scene: A smith holds up a bright gold coin from a river
beats.summary: Anger: one whom the wise praise day after day is like pure gold, and who can blame such a person?

beats.scene: A monk walks slowly with folded hands and lowered eyes along a quiet lane
beats.summary: Anger: guard against anger of body, speech and mind, for the wise are restrained in all three.

beats.scene: A withered yellow leaf drifts down toward a signpost at a crossroads
beats.summary: Impurity: you are now like a withered leaf, so make an island for yourself and strive quickly.

beats.scene: A smith picks silver dross from a crucible with tongs
beats.summary: Impurity: the wise remove their impurities little by little, as a smith removes dross from silver.

beats.scene: An old iron sword covered with rust in a dim storeroom
beats.summary: Impurity: rust born from iron eats the iron, as a person's own deeds lead to a bad end.

beats.scene: A neglected house with a sagging door beside a dusty bookshelf
beats.summary: Impurity: not studying is the stain of learning, neglect the stain of a home, laziness the stain of beauty, and worst is ignorance.

beats.scene: A bold crow steals bread beside a shy sparrow waiting its turn
beats.summary: Impurity: life is easy for the shameless and bold, and hard for the modest who seek purity.

beats.scene: A man digs around the roots of his own tree until it leans
beats.summary: Impurity: whoever harms living beings, lies, steals or loses himself in drink digs up his own root.

beats.scene: A gambler hides a losing die behind his back while pointing at another
beats.summary: Impurity: other people's faults are easy to see and our own are hard, and we hide them like a cheating gambler.

beats.scene: A judge listens carefully to two neighbours before speaking
beats.summary: The Just: one who decides in haste is not just, and a just judge weighs both sides.

beats.scene: A loud speaker holds a crowd while a quiet woman practises kindness
beats.summary: The Just: talking a great deal does not make a person wise, since the wise are peaceful and free from hate and fear.

beats.scene: An old man with grey hair, restless, sits near a calm young woman
beats.summary: The Just: grey hair does not make an elder, but truth, virtue, harmlessness and self-control do.

beats.scene: A beautifully dressed man scowls while a plain woman smiles warmly
beats.summary: The Just: eloquence or looks do not make a person good if envy and deceit remain.

beats.scene: A shaven-headed man with a stern face shouts at a worker
beats.summary: The Just: a shaved head does not make a monk, but calming evil, large and small, does.

beats.scene: A woman carries a small child gently across a stream
beats.summary: The Just: one is noble through harmlessness to all beings, and should not rest content with outward practices.

beats.scene: A wide path with eight stone steps rises through a green hillside
beats.summary: The Path: the best of paths is the Noble Eightfold Path and the best of truths the Four Noble Truths.

beats.scene: A teacher points down a road while a student takes the first step
beats.summary: The Path: we must make the effort ourselves, for the Buddhas only point the way.

beats.scene: Autumn leaves fall from a tree beside a quiet river
beats.summary: The Path: all made things are impermanent, and seeing this with wisdom leads to purity.

beats.scene: A strong young man sleeps late in the sun beside an unploughed field
beats.summary: The Path: one who does not strive when it is time to strive never finds the way to wisdom.

beats.scene: A man sits with lips closed and hands still in a quiet garden
beats.summary: The Path: watch your speech, guard your mind and do nothing harmful with the body.

beats.scene: A student studies by lamplight, then rests in silent thought
beats.summary: The Path: from meditation wisdom springs and without it wisdom fades, so follow the way that makes wisdom grow.

beats.scene: A woodcutter clears dense undergrowth from the edge of a thick forest
beats.summary: The Path: cut down the forest of desire, not only one tree, because while any undergrowth remains the mind is bound.

beats.scene: A man plans a house for every season as a storm gathers
beats.summary: The Path: the fool plans to stay here in rain, summer and winter, not seeing the danger.

beats.scene: A great flood sweeps through a sleeping village at night
beats.summary: The Path: death carries off the heedless like a flood a sleeping village, and no relative can hold it back.

beats.scene: A boy gives up a small sweet to share in a feast
beats.summary: Miscellaneous: give up a smaller happiness to gain a greater one.

beats.scene: A man laughs while a neighbour cries, both tied by a rope of anger
beats.summary: Miscellaneous: seeking happiness by causing suffering to others entangles one in hatred.

beats.scene: A craftsman's tools gather dust while he sits idle
beats.summary: Miscellaneous: what should be done is left undone and what should not be done is done, while the mindful lose their taints.

beats.scene: Monks watch the dawn sky from a hilltop
beats.summary: Miscellaneous: the always-awake recall day and night the Buddha, the teaching, the community, the body, harmlessness and meditation.

beats.scene: A snow peak rises above a faraway village at sunrise
beats.summary: Miscellaneous: a person of faith and virtue is honoured everywhere, and the good shine from afar like the Himalaya.

beats.scene: A solitary hut stands at a forest edge with smoke rising
beats.summary: Miscellaneous: one who sits alone, walks alone and tames himself alone finds delight at the forest's edge.

beats.scene: A man turns away from an open ledger in a dim room
beats.summary: Hell: one who lies, or who does wrong and denies it, comes to sorrow, and the chapter names this hell.

beats.scene: A hand grips a blade of sharp grass the wrong way
beats.summary: Hell: kusa grass wrongly grasped cuts the hand, so do whatever is to be done with full effort.

beats.scene: Guards walk the walls of a border city at night
beats.summary: Hell: a wrong deed is better left undone, so guard yourself like a border city and let no moment pass.

beats.scene: A man hides from something harmless and ignores a real danger
beats.summary: Hell: being ashamed of the wrong things and fearing the wrong things is wrong view, and seeing fault as fault is right view.

beats.scene: An elephant stands calmly on a dusty field while arrows fall around it
beats.summary: The Elephant: I will bear insults as an elephant in battle bears arrows, for a tamed elephant carries a king.

beats.scene: A king rides a calm elephant while mules and horses wait behind
beats.summary: The Elephant: mules, horses and elephants are fine, but one who has tamed himself is best.

beats.scene: A mahout guides a large elephant with a gentle hook along a river path
beats.summary: The Elephant: once the mind wandered as it pleased, and now I hold it as a mahout holds an elephant, so lift yourself out of the mud.

beats.scene: A lone elephant walks calmly through a quiet forest at dusk
beats.summary: The Elephant: walk with a wise companion if you find one, and if not, walk alone like an elephant in the forest.

beats.scene: Friends help each other carry a heavy load up a hill
beats.summary: The Elephant: good are friends in need, contentment, kindness to parents and virtue lasting to old age.

beats.scene: A thick green creeper climbs and wraps itself around a tall tree
beats.summary: Craving: craving grows like a creeping vine in the heedless, and the heedless leap like a monkey seeking fruit.

beats.scene: Tall weeds spring up thick in a field after heavy rain
beats.summary: Craving: sorrows grow like grass after rain in one overcome by craving, and fall away from one who overcomes it.

beats.scene: A gardener digs deep around a stubborn grass root
beats.summary: Craving: dig up the root of craving, for a cut tree grows again if its root is sound.

beats.scene: A hare darts in panic across a field toward a hunter's snare
beats.summary: Craving: people bound by craving run like a snared hare.

beats.scene: An iron chain, a rope and a necklace of jewels lie side by side
beats.summary: Craving: the wise say the strongest bond is not iron or rope but longing for jewels and loved ones.

beats.scene: A spider rests in the middle of its own web at dawn
beats.summary: Craving: the lustful fall into the stream they have made, like a spider in its own web, and the wise cut it and go on.

beats.scene: A traveller stands at a river's edge and leaves a heavy pack behind
beats.summary: Craving: let go of the past, the future and what lies between, and cross to the far shore.

beats.scene: Weeds crowd a field of ripening grain near a farmer's hands
beats.summary: Craving: the gift of the teaching excels all gifts, and as weeds spoil fields, passion spoils people.

beats.scene: A monk sits with lowered eyes in a quiet courtyard, listening
beats.summary: The Monk: restraint of eye, ear, nose and tongue is good, and restraint everywhere frees from suffering.

beats.scene: A monk speaks softly to a group of children under a tree
beats.summary: The Monk: one controlled in hand, foot and speech, content and alone, speaks sweetly.

beats.scene: A monk accepts a small bowl of rice with a calm face
beats.summary: The Monk: do not despise what you receive or envy what others gain, for those who envy lose their calm.

beats.scene: A monk bails water out of a small wooden boat on a calm lake
beats.summary: The Monk: empty your boat and it will go lightly, and cutting off greed and hatred leads to freedom.

beats.scene: A student sits by a window with an open book and closed eyes
beats.summary: The Monk: meditate and do not be careless, for there is no meditation without wisdom and no wisdom without meditation.

beats.scene: A monk sits in a quiet empty hut as sunlight falls on the floor
beats.summary: The Monk: in a quiet place a calm mind finds a joy beyond the ordinary.

beats.scene: A jasmine bush drops withered flowers on the ground
beats.summary: The Monk: as jasmine sheds its withered flowers, so shed lust and hatred.

beats.scene: A merchant gently brushes and steadies a fine horse
beats.summary: The Monk: reprove yourself and guard yourself, as a merchant looks after a fine horse.

beats.scene: A person stands on a river bank between two shores
beats.summary: The Brahmin: cut off the stream, and the one who needs neither shore is fearless and unbound.

beats.scene: The sun, the moon and a warrior in armour shine beside a meditating figure
beats.summary: The Brahmin: the sun shines by day, the moon by night and the warrior in armour, but the Buddha shines always.

beats.scene: A calm woman puts down a basket and speaks to no one
beats.summary: The Brahmin: one who has put away evil, and does no harm by body, speech or mind, is truly noble.

beats.scene: A calm traveller in plain clothes is greeted at a village gate
beats.summary: The Brahmin: one is noble not by matted hair, family or birth, but by truth and righteousness.

beats.scene: A man with tangled hair and an antelope skin stands by a stream
beats.summary: The Brahmin: what use are matted hair and a deerskin cloak when the tangle is within?

beats.scene: A thin man in patched robes meditates alone under a tree
beats.summary: The Brahmin: the one with nothing and no clinging is noble, and birth does not make one so.

beats.scene: A man stands calmly as people shout and jeer at him
beats.summary: The Brahmin: one who bears abuse and blows without anger, whose strength is patience, is noble.

beats.scene: A woman lays a staff on the ground and offers peace
beats.summary: The Brahmin: one who has laid down violence to all beings is friendly among the hostile and peaceful among the violent.

beats.scene: A teacher speaks kindly to a student beside a lost coin left untouched
beats.summary: The Brahmin: one who speaks gentle, true words and takes nothing not given is noble.

beats.scene: A full moon shines on a still, spotless pond
beats.summary: The Brahmin: one who is beyond clinging to good and evil is spotless like the moon.

beats.scene: A traveller crosses a muddy road and steps onto firm dry ground
beats.summary: The Brahmin: one who has crossed the muddy, dangerous road of delusion to the other shore walks free.

beats.scene: A woman sets down a heavy bundle by the roadside and breathes freely
beats.summary: The Brahmin: one who has put down the burden and done what was to be done is at peace.

beats.scene: Drops of water roll off a lotus leaf on a still pond at sunrise
beats.summary: The Brahmin: the free person clings to no pleasure, like water on a lotus leaf, and the book ends by inviting each reader to walk on.

A1A2: The Dhammapada is a book of short sayings from the Buddhist tradition.
Each verse is short, so you can read one and think about it.
Everything begins in the mind, so an angry mind brings pain.
A kind mind brings happiness, and happiness follows like a shadow.
A blind monk walked slowly and stepped on tiny insects by mistake.
Those who keep counting old wrongs never find peace.
Hate cannot stop hate, but love can stop it.
Many people forget that life is short, so they fight.
A weak tree bends in the wind, but a mountain stands firm.
A monk's robe has meaning only if the monk is honest.
People who value the wrong things never find what matters.
Rain comes through a bad roof, and bad wants enter a careless mind.
A person who does wrong is sad, and a person who does good is glad.
Reading many books does not help if you never practise them.
Being awake and careful in every moment leads to true peace.
The wise know this, so they love to stay careful and alert.
A wise person makes an island that no flood can cover.
A slow student learned a great deal from one clean white cloth.
Fools waste their days, but the wise guard care like treasure.
The wise person climbs high and looks calmly down at the struggling crowd.
The wise stay awake while others sleep and move on like fast horses.
A monk who loves care burns his chains away like fire.
A wise person makes the mind straight as a man makes an arrow straight.
A fish pulled from water jumps and shakes on dry ground.
A mind that is trained and calm brings real happiness.
The mind is hard to see, and it travels far alone.
A jumping mind cannot learn wisdom, but a calm mind has no fear.
Know that the body is a fragile jar, and guard the mind.
Soon the body will lie still on the ground like a log.
A wrong thought can hurt you more than an enemy can.
A learner picks the best teaching like a gardener picks flowers.
Death can come like a flood to a sleeping village.
A bee takes honey from a flower and does not hurt it.
Look at your own deeds, not at the faults of others.
Fine words without good deeds are like a flower with no scent.
From a pile of flowers many garlands can be made.
The scent of flowers goes with the wind, but goodness goes everywhere.
A lotus can grow sweet on a rubbish heap, and so can wisdom.
The night is long for a person who cannot sleep.
It is better to walk alone than with a foolish friend.
A fool worries about his children and his money, but nothing lasts for ever.
A fool who knows he is a fool is already a little wise.
A spoon sits in the soup all day but never tastes it.
A deed that makes you cry later was not a good deed.
Wrongdoing seems sweet like honey until its fruit is ripe.
A proud fool wants fame and the best seat at every feast.
One road leads to gain, and another leads to peace.
Be glad of a person who shows you your mistakes.
Keep good friends, and stay away from bad friends.
Those who drink in the teaching live happily with a clear mind.
A young novice watched craftsmen and learned to train his own mind.
Praise and blame cannot move the wise, as wind cannot move rock.
After hearing the teaching, the wise become calm like a clear lake.
The wise are not too happy or too sad when life changes.
Few people cross the river, and most run along the bank.
The wise leave the dark road and walk the bright road.
For the one who has finished the journey, there is no more sorrow.
Like swans leaving a lake, the free do not cling to a home.
A bird crosses the sky and leaves no track behind.
Even the gods admire a person who has tamed the senses.
He is patient like the earth and does not get angry.
Where the calm and free live, any place is a delightful place.
One word that brings peace is better than a thousand empty words.
The greatest winner is the person who wins over himself.
One moment of respect for a good person is worth more than costly gifts.
Respect for older people helps life, beauty, happiness and strength grow.
One day lived with care is better than a hundred careless years.
One day of real effort is better than a hundred lazy years.
One day of seeing how things change beats a hundred years of not seeing.
A mother who lost her baby learned that every home knows death.
One day of seeing the highest truth beats a hundred years without it.
Do good things quickly, before the mind turns to bad things.
Do not repeat a wrong, but repeat every good thing you do.
Results take time, so keep doing good even when you wait.
Drop by drop, an empty water pot slowly becomes full.
A rich traveller avoids a dangerous road, and a wise person avoids evil.
Harm done to a good person comes back like dust in the wind.
There is no place in the world to hide from your own deeds.
Everyone is afraid of pain, so do not hurt other people.
Hurting others to be happy never works, but kindness does.
Harsh words come back to you, so speak to everyone kindly.
A broken gong makes no noise, and a calm person makes no quarrel.
Old age and death drive our lives on, as a boy drives cows.
Ashes and dirt do not make a person pure; a gentle heart does.
A good horse moves at the lightest touch, and so should we.
Why only play and laugh, when we could look for a light?
This body looks lovely, but it is fragile and always changing.
The body is a house of bones, and pride lives in it too.
Even a king's fine chariot wears out, and so does the body.
A person who has learned very little grows old like an ox in a field.
The builder of the house is craving, and it will build no more.
Those who waste their youth are sad when they grow old.
If you love yourself, guard yourself and practise before you teach.
Teach others by living as you teach, and tame yourself first.
You are your own refuge, and nobody else can take your place.
Bad deeds are easy to do, but good deeds are hard.
We make ourselves pure; no one else can do it for us.
Help others, but do not forget your own real good.
Wake up, do not be lazy, and follow the good path.
See the world as a bubble, and hold it with a light hand.
A feared robber met the Buddha, gave up harm and became a monk.
The world is blind, and few people see the truth clearly.
Swans follow the path of the sun across the sky.
A liar who respects nothing may do any wrong.
The first step toward freedom is better than ruling the earth.
The Buddha's victory cannot be undone, and nothing holds him back.
The wise find joy in quiet meditation, and even the gods admire them.
Being a person is rare, and hearing the teaching is rare.
Do no wrong, do good, and make your mind clean.
Patience is the highest discipline, say the awakened ones.
A rain of gold coins could never satisfy our wants.
Fear sends people to many places, but wisdom is the safest refuge.
A Buddha is hard to find, and his birth is a blessing.
Honour those who deserve honour, for that goodness cannot be measured.
Let us live happily and hate no one, even among haters.
Let us live happily without owning much, and feed on joy.
A winner makes enemies, but a peaceful person is happy.
Hunger is the worst illness, and peace is the highest happiness.
Good health is the best gift, and being content is the best wealth.
A person who has tasted quiet peace is free from fear.
Walk with the wise, as the moon walks among the stars.
Being apart from loved ones hurts, and so does meeting people we dislike.
Holding things too tightly hurts us when they are gone.
Too much clinging to people brings sorrow and fear.
A grandmother cried for a lost little girl and learned about clinging.
People love a person who is honest, kind and does his duty.
Friends welcome a traveller home, and good deeds welcome a good person.
Let go of anger and pride, and you will be free.
A wise person stops anger the way a driver stops a runaway cart.
Beat anger with kindness, and beat lies with truth.
Tell the truth, do not be angry, and give even a little.
No one is always praised, and no one is always blamed.
A person praised by the wise is like pure gold.
Guard your body, your speech and your mind from anger.
Like an old leaf, we must make our island while there is time.
The wise clean their minds little by little, as a smith cleans silver.
Rust grows from iron and slowly eats the iron itself.
Not studying spoils learning, and not caring spoils a house.
The shameless have an easy life, but the modest find it hard.
A person who harms, lies or steals digs up his own roots.
Other people's faults are easy to see, but our own are not.
A fair judge listens to both sides before he decides.
A person is not wise just because he talks a great deal.
Grey hair does not make an elder, but a good heart does.
A kind heart is more beautiful than a beautiful face.
A shaved head does not make a monk; peace in the heart does.
A truly noble person does no harm to any living thing.
Of all the paths, the Eightfold Path is the best.
You must make the effort yourself, because teachers only show the way.
All made things change, and seeing this brings wisdom and peace.
A strong young person who is lazy will never find wisdom.
Watch your words, guard your mind and do no harm with your body.
Quiet thought brings wisdom, and a hurried mind loses it.
Cut down the forest of wanting, not only a single tree.
A fool plans for every season and does not see the danger.
When death comes, family cannot hold it back, so use your days well.
Give up a small joy if it lets you gain a bigger one.
Hurting others to be happy only ties us to hatred.
Some people ignore what they should do and do what they should not.
The Buddha's followers wake each day and recall the teaching.
Good people shine from far away, like mountains in the sun.
A calm person who trains himself alone finds joy at the forest edge.
Lying brings sorrow, and so does hiding what you have done.
Hold sharp grass the wrong way and it cuts your hand.
Guard yourself like a city, and do not waste the moment.
Seeing wrong as wrong and right as right leads to a good road.
I will bear insults like an elephant bears arrows in a battle.
A tamed mule or horse is fine, but a tamed self is best.
My mind once wandered where it liked, but now I guide it.
If you find no good friend, walk alone like an elephant in the forest.
It is good to have friends, to be content and to honour parents.
Wanting more and more grows like a weed in a careless mind.
Sorrows grow like weeds in a person who is full of wants.
Dig out the root of craving, so that it cannot grow again.
A person full of wants runs around like a frightened hare.
The strongest chain is not iron but the longing for things.
A spider can be caught in its own web, and so can we.
Let go of the past, the future and the time in between.
The gift of the teaching is better than every other gift.
Guard the eye, the ear, the nose and the tongue.
A calm person controls his hands, his feet and his words.
Be glad of what you receive, and do not envy other people.
Empty the boat, and it will move lightly across the water.
You need wisdom to meditate well, and you need meditation to gain wisdom.
A calm mind in a quiet place finds a joy beyond the ordinary.
As a jasmine plant drops old flowers, we can drop old anger.
Examine yourself honestly, and keep yourself in check like a fine horse.
The last chapter describes the noble person who has crossed the river.
The sun shines by day, the moon by night, and the wise by thought.
A person who does no harm in body, speech or mind is noble.
We are noble because of our actions, not because of our birth.
What good is long hair if the trouble is inside you?
A person with no possessions and no clinging is truly free.
A noble person bears insults and blows without getting angry.
A noble person is friendly even to those who are not.
A noble person speaks gently and truly, and takes nothing that is not given.
A noble person is pure and calm like the full moon.
A noble person has crossed the muddy road and stands on dry ground.
A noble person has put down the heavy load and is at peace.
The free person does not cling, like water on a lotus leaf.
B1B2: The Dhammapada is a collection of 423 short verses arranged in 26 chapters. They are part of the Pali Canon, an early collection of Buddhist scriptures, and Buddhists everywhere have loved them for centuries.
Each verse is short enough to remember, and many people learn them by heart. Tradition says that a story was told for each one, and a few of those stories appear here.
The first chapter says that the mind comes before everything we do. If we speak or act with an angry mind, suffering follows us, as a wheel follows the ox.
The next verse shows the same law working in the opposite direction, toward joy. When we speak or act with a clear and kind mind, happiness follows us like a shadow that never leaves.

Tradition tells of Cakkhupala, a blind monk who walked up and down each morning. Without knowing it he stepped on small insects, but the Buddha said he was not to blame, because his mind had meant no harm.

Some people keep saying, “He insulted me, he hurt me, he cheated me,” and they repeat it for years. The verse says that hatred never ends for those who keep thinking this way, but it does end for those who let the thoughts go.
One of the best-known verses says that hatred is never ended by hatred. Only love can end it, and the verse calls this an old and lasting truth.
Another verse says that many people forget that we must all die one day. Those who do remember it find that their quarrels begin to end.

A person who chases pleasure, eats too much and never controls the senses is shaken by temptation like a weak tree in the wind. A person who is careful, moderate and faithful stays firm, as a mountain of rock cannot be moved by the wind.

A person may put on the plain yellow robe of a monk and still be full of dirt inside. The verse says that the robe belongs to the one who is honest and self-controlled, for goodness is not a matter of clothes.

Some people take what is unimportant for important, and what is truly important for unimportant. They live with wrong thoughts, so they never reach the heart of things, but those who see clearly do reach it.
If a roof is badly made, rain will leak into the house. In the same way, desire breaks into an untrained mind, but it cannot enter a mind that has been well developed.
The wrongdoer grieves now and grieves later, and he suffers when he sees the harm he has done. The doer of good is glad now and glad later, and he rejoices at the sight of his own good deeds.
A person may recite a great many holy texts but never act on them. Such a person is like a cowherd who counts another man's cows and has no share in the herd.
The second chapter praises heedfulness, which means paying close attention to what we think and do. It says that attention leads to the deathless, while those who are careless are as good as dead.
Those who understand this are glad to be careful, and they take joy in the way of the noble. They are thoughtful, steady and honest, and they live carefully, so their good name grows.
By effort, care and self-control, says the Dhammapada, a wise person can build an island. No flood will ever be able to cover it.

Tradition tells of Culapanthaka, who found it so hard to learn even one verse that his own brother sent him away. The Buddha gave him a clean white cloth to rub, and as it grew dirty in his hands he understood how all things change.

Foolish people give themselves to carelessness, but the wise guard their attention as their greatest treasure. They do not give way to carelessness or to pleasure, and in quiet meditation they find great happiness.
Picture a person on a mountain, looking down at the crowd on the plain. In the same way, the wise climb the tower of wisdom by care, and from there they look calmly on those who struggle.
Among those who are careless, the wise person stays careful, and among those who sleep, he stays awake. He moves ahead like a swift horse that leaves a weak one far behind.
A monk who delights in care, and who sees danger in carelessness, moves forward like a fire. He burns every bond, small and large, and he is close to freedom and cannot easily fall away.
The third chapter is about the mind, which it calls restless and hard to guard. Just as a maker of arrows straightens each arrow, the wise person slowly straightens the mind.
The mind, says the Dhammapada, is like a fish that has been thrown onto dry land. It twists and shakes whenever we try to pull it out of its old habits, but we should keep trying.
The mind is hard to hold, because it flies wherever it wishes. But a mind that has been tamed and trained brings happiness to its owner.
The mind is very subtle and hard to see, and it goes wherever it likes. Wise people guard it, because a guarded mind brings happiness, and they say the mind lives in the cave of the heart.
A person whose mind is unsteady and whose faith wavers will not become wise. But one whose mind is free from craving and from anger has no reason to be afraid.
Know that this body is as fragile as a clay jar, and make the mind as strong as a fortified city. Fight the tempter with the weapon of wisdom, and then guard what you have won.
Before long, this body will lie on the earth, without life or thought, like a log that nobody wants. The verse is not meant to frighten us, but to help us use our days well.
An enemy can do us harm, and so can a person who hates us. Yet a badly directed mind harms us even more, and a well-directed mind helps us more than our own parents can.
The fourth chapter is called Flowers, and it asks who will master this world and the next. The learner, it answers, will choose the well-taught lesson as a skilled gardener chooses the best flowers.
The verses say that the body is like foam on water, and like a mirage. Death carries off a person who is busy gathering flowers, as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village.

The fourth chapter is called Flowers, and one of its pictures shows a bee at work. The bee takes its nectar and flies away without harming the flower, and the wise walk through villages in the same gentle way.
Do not spend your days looking at what other people have done or failed to do. Look at your own deeds, at what you have done and what you have left undone.
A flower can be bright and beautiful and still have no scent. Fine words are like that when no deeds follow them, but they bear fruit when deeds match them.
From one great heap of flowers, a skilled person can make many garlands. In the same way, one short life can be used to do a great deal of good.
The scent of flowers, or even of sandalwood, cannot travel against the wind. However, the fragrance of a good person spreads in every direction, even against the wind.
Beside the highway there may be a heap of rubbish, and from it a sweet lotus may rise. In the same way, among blind and careless people the follower of the awakened one shines brightly with wisdom.
The fifth chapter is about the fool, a person who does not learn from life. The night seems long to the sleepless and the road long to the tired, and so is life to those who ignore the truth.
If a traveller cannot find a companion who is better or at least equal, he should go on alone. A fool cannot be a good companion on the road.
A fool is troubled day and night by thoughts of my children and my wealth. But even the self is not ours to hold for ever, so how much less are our children and our riches?
A fool who knows that he is a fool is, to that extent, already wise. The fool who thinks he is wise, however, is the one who is truly called a fool.
A spoon may sit in a bowl of soup for a lifetime and never taste it. In the same way, a fool who lives near a wise person may never understand the teaching.

Foolish people act as their own worst enemies, because they do wrong and then taste the bitter fruit. A deed is badly done if we regret it and weep, and it is well done if we feel no regret and are glad.
To the fool, wrongdoing tastes as sweet as honey while its result is still hidden. When the result ripens he comes to grief, for a wrong deed follows him like a fire that smoulders under ashes.

The fool wants a great name that he has not earned, the first place among others and honour wherever he goes. He wants everyone to think that all good work was done by him, and so his pride and his desires only grow.
One road leads to gain, and another road leads to freedom. Knowing this, a follower of the Buddha should not take delight in honour but should look for quiet and solitude.
Imagine that a stranger shows you where a great treasure is buried. The Dhammapada says that a friend who shows us our faults is just as valuable, and that we should follow him.

A wise person gives advice, teaches and holds others back from wrong, and good people love him for it, though bad people do not. So we should not keep bad friends or the lowest kind of company, but should keep good friends and the best of company.
A person who drinks in the teaching lives happily, with a mind that is calm and clear. The wise always take pleasure in the teaching of the noble, as a thirsty traveller enjoys cool water.

Farmers lead water where they want it, arrow makers straighten shafts, and carpenters shape wood. The wise, says the verse, tame themselves, and tradition links it to Pandita, a young novice who learned this lesson from watching such workers.
A solid rock is not shaken by the wind, however hard it blows. In the same way, a wise person is not moved by either praise or blame.
Like a deep lake that is clear and still, the wise grow calm after they have heard the teachings. Their minds become quiet, and in that stillness they see things as they really are.
Good people let go of what they hold, and they do not chatter about their wants. When happiness or sorrow touches them, the wise show no great joy and no deep despair.
Among all human beings, only a few ever reach the far shore of the river. Most of the others only run up and down along the near bank, busy but never crossing.

Those who follow the teaching well will cross the river that is so hard to cross. They leave the dark way for the bright, they find joy in quiet places, and they cleanse the mind of everything that clouds it.
The seventh chapter describes the arahant, a person who has reached the end of the path. For him the journey is over, and he is free from sorrow and from every kind of bond.
Those who are mindful keep trying, and they take no delight in any one place as their home. Like swans that leave a lake, they leave each house behind them, without sorrow.
Those who store up nothing, who eat only what they need and who are free in mind, leave no track that anyone can follow. They are like birds flying across the sky, whose paths cannot be traced.
The senses are like horses, and a good charioteer tames them until they are calm. Even the gods, says the verse, admire a person who has done this and who has no pride left.
Such a person is patient like the earth, which does not resent anyone who walks across it. He is steady like a pillar, and he is like a lake without mud, calm and clear.

Calm are the thoughts, the words and the deeds of a person who is free through right understanding. Wherever such people live, in a village or a forest, in a valley or on a hill, that place is delightful.
The eighth chapter is called Thousands, and it compares large numbers with small ones. Better than a thousand empty words, it says, is a single word that brings peace to whoever hears it.
Imagine a man who defeats a thousand thousand men in battle, one after another. The verse says that someone who conquers himself is a far greater winner than he is.
A person might spend a hundred years making costly offerings, month after month. Yet one moment of honest respect for someone who has trained his mind is worth more than all of them.
A person who is respectful and who always honours the elders will see four things grow. They are length of life, beauty, happiness and strength, say the verses.
Better than a hundred years lived without virtue or thought is a single day lived with virtue and meditation. Better, too, is one day lived wisely than a hundred years lived like a fool.
Better than a hundred years of laziness and weak effort is a single day of firm and steady effort. The verse praises the energy that gets a person up in the morning and sets him to work.
Better than a hundred years without noticing how things arise and pass away is one day of seeing it clearly. Everything we know is like a wave that rises, falls and is followed by another.

Tradition links this verse to Kisa Gotami, a young mother who carried her dead baby from door to door, hoping for a cure. The Buddha asked for a mustard seed from a house where no one had died, and her search taught her that death visits every family.
Better than a hundred years of life without seeing the highest teaching is one day of seeing it. The chapter ends with this last comparison, which tells us that depth matters more than length.
The ninth chapter tells us to hurry to do good and to hold the mind back from evil. If we are slow to do good, it warns, the mind will begin to enjoy doing wrong.
If a person does wrong, he should not repeat it or set his heart on it, because piling up wrongs brings pain. If he does good, he should repeat it often, because piling up good brings happiness.
Even a wrongdoer may see good days for a while, as long as his wrong deed has not ripened. And even a good person may see hard days, until the good deed bears its fruit.
Never think lightly of wrongdoing by saying that it will not come back to you. A water jar is filled drop by drop, and so we are filled, little by little, with good or with evil.

A merchant with a small escort and great wealth avoids a dangerous road, and a person who loves life avoids poison. In the same way, we should avoid evil, for poison cannot enter a hand that has no wound.
Whoever harms a person who is innocent and blameless will see the harm come back. It returns to that fool like fine dust that has been thrown against the wind.
Not in the sky, nor in the sea, nor in a mountain cave can a person escape the results of an evil deed. There is no place on earth where anyone can stand and be safe from what he has done.
The tenth chapter says that everyone is afraid of violence, and that everyone loves life. If we imagine ourselves in the place of others, we will not wish to hurt any living being.

Every living being wants to be happy, and the verse says that this is the one thing we share. Whoever seeks happiness by harming others who also want it will not find it, but whoever harms no one will.
Do not speak harshly to anyone, because the people you speak to will answer you in the same way. Angry words cause pain, and the blows of retaliation will touch you in return.
If you can make yourself as still as a broken gong, which no longer rings, you have already reached peace. In such a person no anger can be found, and there is no quarrel left to fight.
A cowherd uses his stick to drive his cows toward the pasture. In the same way, old age and death drive the lives of all living things before them.

Going without clothes, wearing matted hair, fasting and covering oneself with ashes do not make a person pure. Even a person in fine clothes is a true holy person if he is calm, restrained and kind to every living being.
A good horse needs only the lightest touch of the whip to move forward. In the same way, the verse says, we should be eager and thoughtful, with faith, virtue, effort and understanding.
The eleventh chapter asks why we laugh and play when the world is burning with wants. We live in darkness, so why do we not look for a light?
Look at this decorated body, says the verse, which is so often ill and so full of plans. It is fragile and worn by time, and it cannot last for ever.
The body is like a house built with bones as its frame and covered with flesh and skin. Inside this house we find ageing, death, pride and deceit, all living side by side.
The eleventh chapter speaks about growing old, and it does so without fear. Even a splendid royal chariot wears out, and so does the body, but the teaching of the good never grows old.
A person who has learned little grows old like an ox. His body grows bigger, but his wisdom does not grow at all.
Tradition says that at his awakening the Buddha spoke of a house-builder, which is his name for craving. He said that its rafters were broken, and that it would never build a house for him again.
People who did not use their youth well sit in old age like herons beside a pond without fish. They lie like broken bows, sighing for what is past.
If you hold yourself dear, guard yourself well, as a night guard keeps watch through the dark. First do what is right yourself, and then teach others, so that you will not suffer for it.
A person should act as he teaches others to act. If he has tamed himself well, he can help others to do the same, although taming the self is hard.
You yourself are your own refuge, for who else could be? When you have trained yourself well, you find a safe place that is very hard to find.

Wrong done by a person comes from himself and wears him down, like a hard diamond cutting a softer stone. A person with no virtue is like a creeper that strangles a tree, for he does to himself what an enemy would wish.

By ourselves we do wrong, and by ourselves we become unclean, says the verse. In the same way, we make ourselves pure, because purity and impurity belong to each person and no one can cleanse another.
However much you do for others, do not lose sight of your own real good. Once you know what is truly good for you, set your mind firmly on the highest goal.
The thirteenth chapter, called The World, begins with a loud call to wake up. It tells us to get up, to be careful and to follow the good path, which brings happiness.
The verse tells us to look upon the world as a bubble or a mirage. It also calls the world a painted royal chariot, in which fools sink while the wise feel no attachment.

Tradition links this verse to Angulimala, a robber who was feared in the countryside until he met the Buddha and gave up violence. One who was careless before and is careful later, says the verse, lights up the world like the moon freed from a cloud.
The verse says that this world is blind and that only a few see clearly. Just as only a few birds escape from a net, only a few people reach a happy state.
Swans fly along the path of the sun, and the verse says that the wise rise up in a similar way. They go beyond the world after they have conquered the tempter and all his army.
A person who lies and who respects nothing can bring himself to do any wrong. Misers do not praise giving, but the wise delight in it and are happy because of it.

Better than ruling the whole earth, or going to heaven, or being lord of all the worlds, is the first great step on the path. This step is called stream-entry, because the person has joined the current that flows toward freedom.

The fourteenth chapter, called The Buddha, praises one whose victory can never be undone and whom nothing in the world can follow. No craving is left in him, so by what path could anyone lead him back?
Those who are wise take joy in meditation and in the peace of leaving worldly things behind. Even the gods, says the verse, hold dear the ones who are awake and mindful.
The same chapter says that it is hard to be born as a human being, and hard to live a mortal life. It is also hard to hear the true teaching, and hard for a Buddha to appear in the world.
One verse in the chapter on the Buddha is often called a short summary of the whole teaching. It says that we should avoid all evil, do good, and purify our own minds.
Patience, the verse says, is the highest discipline, and freedom is the highest goal. A person who harms others is not a true monk, and one who hurts others is not a true seeker.
Not even a shower of gold coins could satisfy our desires, which give little taste and much pain. The wise know this, and so they find joy in the end of craving instead.
When people are afraid, they run to hills, forests and old trees for shelter. The verse says that a safer shelter is the Buddha, the teaching and the community, with a clear view of the four truths.
A Buddha is very hard to find, and he is not born in every place. The verse calls it a blessing when one appears, and blessed too are the teaching and the harmony of the community.

To honour those who are worthy of honour, such as the Buddhas and their followers, is a very good deed. Its worth cannot be measured by anyone, because those people have overcome every obstacle and crossed beyond sorrow.

The fifteenth chapter is called Happiness, and its first verses are about freedom from hate. It says that we can live happily without hatred even among people who hate, and without worry even among those who worry.
Let us live happily, we who own nothing, and let us feed on joy like the shining gods. The verse suggests that a light heart is worth more than a full storeroom.
Victory breeds hatred, and the one who is defeated lives on in pain and in sorrow. The peaceful live happily, for they have given up both winning and losing.

There is no fire like lust, no crime like hatred, and no happiness greater than peace. Hunger is the worst of illnesses, and a mind that has understood this finds its greatest happiness in Nibbana, the peace of freedom.
Health is the greatest gift, says the Dhammapada, and contentment is the greatest wealth. A trusted person is the best of relatives, and freedom, called Nibbana, is the greatest happiness.
A person who has tasted the sweetness of solitude and the sweetness of peace is free from fear and from evil. He drinks deeply from the joy of the teaching, and he wants nothing more.
It is good to see noble people, and living with them is always a joy, but company with fools brings long sorrow. So follow the wise and patient, as the moon follows the path of the stars.
The sixteenth chapter is called Affection, and it begins by noticing a hard fact of life. Not to see those we love is painful, and to see those we dislike is painful too.
Parting from what we hold dear is painful, the verse says. Those who hold nothing too tightly, neither loved nor disliked, find that nothing binds them.
From clinging affection grief is born, and from affection comes fear. A person who is wholly free from clinging has no grief, so what is there left for him to fear?

Tradition tells of Visakha, a woman who was kind to the monks and who wept when her young granddaughter died. The Buddha is said to have taught her that grief is born from affection, and she slowly found peace.
People hold dear the person who has good character and clear understanding. They love someone who speaks the truth and does his own duty.

When a man has been away for a long time and comes home safely, his relatives and friends welcome him gladly. In the same way, good deeds welcome the one who has done good, when he leaves this world for the next.
The seventeenth chapter, which is about anger, says that we should give up anger and let go of pride. No suffering falls on a person who clings to nothing as his own.
Anger can rise like a chariot that has begun to run away with its driver. The person who stops it quickly, says the verse, is a true charioteer, and the others only hold the reins.
The seventeenth chapter tells us to defeat anger with calm. We should overcome evil with good, a miser with giving, and a liar with the truth.
Speak the truth, do not give way to anger, and give something even if you have only a little. The verse says that these three simple habits lift a person toward a happier state.
An old saying notes that people blame those who sit silent, those who talk a lot and those who speak little. There never was, and never will be, a person who is only blamed or only praised.
But a person whom the wise praise day after day, who is without fault and who is wise and virtuous, is like pure gold. Who could find anything to blame in such a person?
Be careful of anger in the body, and let the body act with restraint. Do the same with speech and with thought, for the wise are well guarded in all three.

The eighteenth chapter, called Impurity, speaks to a person who is like a withered leaf, close to the end of the road. It tells him to make an island for himself, to strive quickly and to become wise, because he has no supplies for the road.
Little by little, moment by moment, a wise person removes his own impurities. A smith cleans the dross from silver in the same patient way.
Rust is born from iron, but then it slowly eats the iron away. In the same way, our own bad deeds lead us toward a sad end.
Not studying is the stain of learning, and not taking care is the stain of a house. Laziness is the stain of beauty, but the worst stain of all is ignorance.
Life is easy for the shameless person, who is as bold as a crow and who pushes others aside. It is harder for the modest person, who always seeks purity and lives without show.

Whoever harms living beings, tells lies, takes what is not given or loses himself in drink is digging up his own roots. Evil habits are hard to control, so do not let greed drag you into long suffering.
It is easy to see the faults of others and hard to see our own. We blow away their faults like chaff, but we hide our own, as a cheating gambler hides a bad throw of the dice.
The nineteenth chapter, called The Just, says that a person who decides a case in haste is not fair. A wise judge weighs both right and wrong, and he treats everyone without favour.
A person does not become wise by speaking a great deal. The wise are peaceful, free from hate and fear, and one who has heard little but lives by it truly knows the teaching.
A person is not an elder just because his head is grey, for he may be only old in years. The true elder is the one who has truth, virtue, kindness and self-control.

A person who is envious, selfish and deceitful does not become admirable by speaking well or by having a fine face. But one who has cut these faults out by the root, and who is wise and free from hatred, is truly beautiful.
A man who is undisciplined and who tells lies does not become a true monk by shaving his head. The one who always calms evil, whether small or great, is called a monk because of that calming.

A person who harms living beings is not noble, but one who is harmless to all of them can be called so. The verse also warns us not to rest content with outward practices, but to keep going until the mind is free.
The twentieth chapter, called The Path, names the best of all paths. It says that the best path is the Noble Eightfold Path and that the best truths are the Four Noble Truths.
The verse says that we ourselves must make the effort, because the Buddhas only point the way. Those who walk the path and keep their minds steady will be freed from the bonds of Mara, the tempter.
All made things change and pass away, and a person who sees this with wisdom grows tired of suffering. This clear seeing, says the verse, is the path that leads to purity.
The time to make an effort is when we are able to do it. A person who is young and strong but lazy, with a weak mind and weak resolve, never finds the way to wisdom.
Be watchful of what you say, keep the mind under control and do nothing harmful with the body. If you keep these three ways of acting clear, you will find the path that the sages made known.
Wisdom grows out of meditation, and without meditation it fades. Knowing these two roads, the one that gains and the one that loses, a person should live so that his wisdom grows.
Cut down the whole forest of desire, and not only a single tree, for fear grows in the forest. As long as even a little undergrowth is left, the mind stays tied, like a calf to its mother.
A fool says, I will live here in the rains, here in the winter and here in the summer. He does not see how soon the plans of every season can end.

The sleeping village and the flood return here, for death carries off those whose minds cling to pleasures. Neither children, parents nor relatives can hold death back, so the wise clear the path to peace without delay.

The twenty-first chapter is a collection of mixed verses, and its first one gives practical advice. If we can see a greater happiness by giving up a lesser one, the wise person gives up the lesser one.
