A person who tries to be happy by causing others to suffer is caught in the ropes of hatred. He will not be freed from it, because he has tied himself to the people he hurts.
In some people what should be done is left undone, and what should not be done is done. Their faults grow, while the faults of those who are mindful and do what is right come to an end.
The verses say that the followers of the Buddha are always well awake. Day and night they remember the Buddha, the teaching and the community, and they delight in kindness and in meditation.
A person who has faith and virtue is honoured wherever he goes. Good people shine from afar like the snowy Himalaya, but bad people go unseen, like arrows shot in the dark.
A person who sits alone, walks alone and works alone, without tiring, can tame himself. He will find his delight at the edge of the forest, in the quiet.
The twenty-second chapter is called Hell, a name for the deep suffering that wrongdoing can bring. It says that a person who tells lies, or who does wrong and then denies it, comes to sorrow.

Sharp grass cuts the hand that grasps it the wrong way, and the verse says that a holy life wrongly handled does the same. A half-hearted deed brings no great fruit, so what is to be done should be done with full effort.

A wrong deed is better left undone, because it torments us afterwards, but a good deed is better done, because we never regret it. Guard yourself as people guard a border city, inside and out, and do not let the moment pass.
Some people feel shame about the wrong things, and some fear the wrong things. They see fault where there is none and miss it where it is, and this is called wrong view.

The twenty-third chapter is named after the elephant, an animal that was trained for battle. Just as an elephant in battle endures the arrows that strike it, says the verse, I will bear the insults of others.
Well-trained mules, fine horses and great elephants are all excellent. But better still is the person who has tamed himself, since no animal can carry us where a trained mind goes.
My mind once wandered wherever it liked, whenever it pleased. Now I will guide it as an elephant driver guides his animal, and I will pull myself out of the mud.
If you find a wise and good friend, walk with him, happy and thoughtful. If you find none, walk alone like an elephant in the forest, doing no harm and wanting little.
Good are friends when we are in need, and good is being content with what we have. Good too is kindness to a mother and a father, and good is a character that stays strong into old age.
The twenty-fourth chapter is about craving, which grows like a creeping vine in the heedless. Dig up its roots, says the verse, as a gardener digs up a weed, so that it cannot grow again and again.
When a person is overcome by fierce craving, his sorrows grow like grass after the rain. But when he overcomes it, his sorrows fall away from him.
Dig up the root of craving, as a gardener digs up a weed with deep roots. A tree grows again after it is cut if its root is sound, and suffering does the same while craving remains.
People who are bound by craving run here and there like a hare in a snare. They are held by their ties and suffer for a long time, so one who wants freedom should put craving away.
The wise do not call a chain of iron, wood or rope the strongest bond. They say the strongest bond is longing for jewels and for loved ones, which looks loose but is hard to break.

Those who are carried away by desire fall into the stream they have made themselves, like a spider in the web it has spun. The wise cut through it, go on without longing and leave all suffering behind.
Let go of what is behind you, let go of what is ahead of you, and let go of what is in between. With a mind that is free everywhere, you will cross to the far shore and not fall back into sorrow.

The gift of the teaching is better than all other gifts, and its taste is better than all other tastes. Weeds spoil a field and passion spoils people, so a gift to those free from passion brings great fruit.

The twenty-fifth chapter, called The Monk, says that restraint is good in the eye, the ear, the nose and the tongue. It is good in body, speech and mind too, and the one who is restrained everywhere is freed from all suffering.
One who controls his hands, his feet and his tongue, and who is content with his own company, is called a monk. His speech is wise and sweet, and he explains the teaching without pride.
A person should not look down on what he has received, and he should not envy what others gain. Those who envy lose their calm, but the one who is content with little is praised even by the gods.
The twenty-fifth chapter is about the monk, who has left home to follow the path. It tells him to empty his boat, because a boat that is empty moves lightly, and to cut off greed and hatred.
Meditate, and do not be careless, and do not let your mind spin about in pleasures. There is no meditation without wisdom and no wisdom without meditation, and one who has both is close to Nibbana.
A monk who has gone into an empty, quiet place and whose mind is at peace feels a joy beyond the ordinary. When he sees clearly how things arise and pass away, he finds a deep gladness.
A jasmine bush lets its withered flowers fall to the ground. In the same way, says the verse, we should let fall our lust and our hatred, completely and for good.

Reprove yourself by yourself, and examine yourself by yourself, and you will live happily, guarded and mindful. You are your own protector and your own refuge, so look after yourself as a merchant looks after a fine horse.
The twenty-sixth and last chapter is called The Brahmin, a word that here means a truly noble person. It tells us to cut off the stream of craving and cross over, and then no fear remains.
The sun shines by day, the moon shines by night, and the warrior shines in his armour. The noble person shines in meditation, but the Buddha shines by day and by night with his own light.

Because he has put away evil, he is called a brahmin, and because he lives in calm, he is called a recluse. One who does no harm by body, speech or mind, and who is restrained in all three, is truly noble.
A person is not made noble by matted hair, by family or by birth, says the verse. Truth and righteousness are what make a person noble, and such a person is truly blessed.
What is the use of matted hair, asks the verse, or of a cloak of antelope skin? The tangle is within, and it is only the outside that is being cleaned.
A thin person in worn robes who meditates alone in the forest is called noble by the verse. Birth does not make anyone noble, for one who owns nothing and clings to nothing is the one who truly is.
One who bears insults, blows and even prison without anger is called noble. His strength is patience, and patience is the army he leads.

One who has laid down violence toward every being, weak or strong, is called noble, and neither kills nor makes others kill. He is friendly among the hostile, peaceful among the violent and free among those who cling.
One who speaks gentle and truthful words that teach and offend no one is called noble. He takes nothing in the world that is not given, whether it is long or short, small or large.
One who has gone beyond clinging to both good and evil, and who is without sorrow and without stain, is called noble. Such a person is pure and calm, like the moon when it is spotless.
One who has passed beyond the muddy and dangerous road of delusion, and has crossed over to the other shore, is called noble. Such a person is steady, free from doubt and free from clinging.
One who knows, even here and now, the end of his own suffering has put down the heavy burden and is free. Such a person has done what was to be done, and nothing more remains to be carried.

The last verses describe a person who clings to nothing, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. That person moves through the world untouched by it, and the book ends by inviting each reader to walk toward the same peace.
C1C2: The Dhammapada is a collection of 423 short verses, set in 26 chapters, that belongs to the Pali Canon, one of the earliest bodies of Buddhist scripture. Its name is often translated as the path of the teaching, and tradition links its verses to the words of the Buddha, who lived in northern India more than two thousand years ago. Each verse is meant to be read slowly and carried into daily life, so this retelling takes its best-loved lines in the order of the chapters.

Nothing in this book needs to be read in a hurry, because each verse is a small thought meant to be carried through the day. Later tradition added a story to explain when and why each one was spoken, and we will visit a few of those stories along the way. The retelling follows the order of the chapters, from the first verses about the mind to the last verses about the free person.

The very first verses of the Dhammapada declare that mind is the forerunner of all things, and that every deed grows out of a thought. Speak or act with a troubled and angry mind, they warn, and suffering will follow as surely as the wheel of a cart follows the hoof of the ox that draws it. The lesson is not meant as a threat but as a plain observation, for what we think quietly today shapes what we do loudly tomorrow.

The second verse mirrors the first and turns the same law toward the light, so that the reader may see both of its faces. When a person speaks or acts with a pure and gentle mind, joy follows as faithfully as a shadow that never leaves its owner. Together the two verses set out the central idea of the whole book: our inner state is the seed, and our life is the harvest.

A later story, told alongside the first verse, concerns a blind monk named Cakkhupala, who paced up and down outside his hut in the early morning. Unable to see them, he trod on some small insects, and other monks found them and told the Buddha. The Buddha answered that no blame could rest on a person who had meant no harm, which is exactly what the verse about the mind had said.

One verse imagines a person who keeps saying that he was insulted, struck, defeated and robbed, and who turns the list over in his mind year after year. Such thoughts, it says, feed the hatred they describe, so that those who dwell on them never see their anger come to an end. Those who refuse to keep the list, by contrast, find that the hatred quietly dies for lack of fuel.

In a verse that has been quoted for many centuries, the teaching says that hatred is never calmed by hatred in this world. It is calmed only by love, and this, the verse adds, is an ancient law that does not change with time or place. Anyone who has answered anger with anger and watched a quarrel grow will recognise the truth of it at once.

Many people quarrel as though life were endless, the verse observes, and they do not remember that everyone must one day die. Those who do remember it, who hold that plain fact steadily in view, find that their quarrels begin to lose their force. It is a sober thought, yet it is offered as a way to a lighter and more peaceful heart.

The Dhammapada sets two people side by side: the first dwells on whatever pleases him, lets his senses run free, eats without measure and is lazy in effort. Mara, the tempter, overthrows such a person with no trouble, as the wind overthrows a frail tree. The second guards the senses, eats in moderation and stays steady in faith and energy, and against him the tempter is as helpless as the wind against a mountain of rock.

The ninth verse looks at the saffron robe worn by Buddhist monks and asks who truly deserves to wear it. A person who has not cast off his own impurities, who lacks honesty and self-control, is not worthy of the robe, however neatly he wears it. The one who has put aside impurity, who is firm in virtue and sincere in speech, is worthy of it, since a uniform can only show what the person inside has already become.

The verses that close this part of the chapter speak of people who mistake the unimportant for the important, and who overlook what is truly important. Because their thoughts are wrongly aimed, they walk past the essence of things the way a man might carry home a sack of husks and leave the grain in the field. Those who see the essential as essential and the useless as useless, by contrast, are guided by right thinking and arrive at what is truly worth having.

As rain leaks through a badly thatched roof, says the verse, so passion breaks into a mind that has not been trained. A mind that has been carefully developed is like a well-thatched house, and no passion can find a way into it, however long the storm. The comparison is practical rather than poetic, for it reminds us that nobody mends a roof while it is raining, and that the time to train the mind is now.

The wrongdoer is sorrowful in this world and in the next, the verses say, and he is troubled whenever he sees how impure his own actions have been. The one who does good, on the other hand, rejoices in both worlds, and the sight of his own pure deeds fills him with delight. The Dhammapada treats conscience here as a kind of weather that follows us everywhere, dark for the one who has done harm and bright for the one who has done good.

Someone may recite a great many sacred texts, the verse says, and yet, careless and heedless, never put a word of them into practice. Such a person is like a cowherd who counts another man's cattle, and he has no part in the true reward of the way. A person who knows only a little, but who lives by it and has let go of greed, hatred and confusion, shares fully in that reward.

The second chapter is a praise of heedfulness, a word that means keeping the mind alert and caring about what one thinks, says and does. Attention, it declares, is the path to the deathless, while carelessness is the road to death, and the careless are as good as dead while they still breathe. The wise understand this difference clearly, and so they take delight in staying awake.

Having understood this clearly, the wise take delight in heedfulness and find joy in the way of the noble ones. They meditate, they persevere, and they reach the great safety from every bond that the verse calls Nibbana. A person who is energetic, mindful, pure in conduct and considerate, who restrains himself and lives by the teaching, sees his good name grow steadily, as a garden grows under daily care.

Through steady effort, careful attention and self-control, the verse says, a wise person can make for himself an island that no flood can overwhelm. The image is memorable because the floods in this teaching are the troubles of life, the waves of anger, fear and loss that sweep over everyone sooner or later. Only the person who has built such an island within can stand on it and remain safe.

A later story tells of Culapanthaka, a monk so slow at learning that after months of trying he still could not remember a single verse, and his own brother told him to go home. The Buddha instead gave him a clean white cloth and asked him to rub it with his hand, repeating a simple phrase about removing dirt. As the cloth grew grey he saw how everything that looks clean will change, and, tradition says, his patient effort carried him to the freedom that cleverness alone had never given him.

Foolish and unwise people, the verses say, give themselves over to carelessness, but the wise guard their attention as a person guards his most precious possession. They refuse to indulge in carelessness or to take delight in sensual pleasures, because they know that a careless moment can undo the work of years. The one who is attentive and meditative, by contrast, reaches a happiness that does not fade.

Imagine a person who stands on a mountain top and looks down at the crowds on the plain far below, the verse says. In the same way, the wise remove carelessness by their own care and climb the high tower of wisdom, where sorrow can no longer reach them. From that height they look without scorn on those who still struggle, for they remember that they too once stood among the crowd.

The wise person is careful among the careless and awake among those who sleep, the verse says, and in that way he moves quickly forward. He is like a swift racehorse that leaves a tired and weak horse behind, not out of pride but because it has somewhere to go. The picture is of a mind that has set its direction and does not wait for the whole crowd to be ready.

The monk who delights in heedfulness and who sees the danger in carelessness, the verses say, goes forward like a fire, burning every bond, small and great, that lies in his way. Such a person is no longer likely to fall away, for he has come close to Nibbana, the freedom of a mind at peace. The chapter ends on this note of safety, as though to promise that steady care, kept up day by day, leads somewhere real.

The third chapter turns to the mind itself, which it describes as trembling, unsteady and hard to guard or to hold in check. Just as a maker of arrows patiently straightens each shaft, the verse says, a wise person straightens the mind. It is a craftsman's task, done a little each day, and it asks for patience far more than for force.

Another verse compares the mind to a fish pulled from its pool and thrown onto dry ground, where it twists and shivers in distress. So the mind struggles, the Dhammapada says, when a person first tries to pull it out of its old habits and into stillness. Anyone who has tried to sit quietly for five minutes will know exactly what the fish is feeling.

The mind is hard to hold and light as a leaf, the verse says, and it settles wherever it wishes, whether or not that place is good for us. A mind that has been tamed, however, is a source of happiness that nothing else can give. For this reason the teaching asks us to train the mind with the same care that a rider gives to a spirited horse.

The mind is subtle and hard to see, the verses say, and it darts wherever it pleases, so the wise guard it with care, for a guarded mind brings happiness. It travels far, alone and without a body, and it makes its home in the cave of the heart. Those who bring it under restraint, the Dhammapada promises, are set free from the bonds of Mara, the tempter.

If the mind is unsteady, the verse says, and a person does not know the true teaching and his faith is always wavering, then his wisdom will never be complete. But the one whose mind is not flooded by craving and whose heart is not troubled by hatred, who has gone beyond both good and bad, is awake and has nothing to fear. The thought is simple: fear lives in the restless mind, and it has no home in a mind that is still.

Know that this body is as fragile as a clay jar, the verse says, and make your mind as strong as a fortified city with high walls and watchful guards. Fight the tempter with the weapon of wisdom, then, and do not rest on the first success. Even after the battle is won, you must go on guarding what you have gained, for a victory that is not watched can be lost as easily as it was won.

Before long, the verse says, this body will lie on the ground, cast aside and empty of mind, like a useless log. It is a hard fact, stated without drama, and it stands among the verses about the mind as a reminder that time is short. The thought is meant to turn our attention from what is passing to what we can still shape today, which is the direction in which the mind is looking.

An enemy may harm an enemy, the Dhammapada notes, and a hater may harm the one he hates, but a mind turned in the wrong direction does far greater damage than either. In the same way, a well-directed mind can do us more good than even a mother or a father could. Everything, in other words, depends on where the mind is pointed, and that is the one thing we can change from within.

The fourth chapter, called Flowers, begins with a question: who will master this earth, and the world of death, and the world of the gods? The learner will do it, the answer comes, in the way a skilled gardener picks out the finest flowers, choosing the well-taught lesson from among the many things a person might hear. The verse suggests that learning is mostly a matter of choosing well, and that a patient eye is worth more than a full basket.

Know that this body is like foam, the verse says, and as fleeting as a mirage, and so break the flower-tipped arrows of the tempter and pass beyond the sight of the king of death. Death carries off the person whose mind is busy gathering flowers, the next verse adds, as a great flood sweeps away a sleeping village. Beauty and pleasure are not wrong in themselves, but a mind that spends all its time gathering them has no time left to wake up.

In the chapter called Flowers, the teaching offers a picture of a bee that visits a blossom, takes its nectar and flies away without damaging its colour or its scent. The sage, the verse says, should go through the village in just the same way, taking what he needs and leaving the place unharmed. It is a lesson in gentleness that asks for no grand gestures, only for a careful and light touch.

Do not look at the faults of others, the verse says, nor at what they have done or left undone. Look instead at your own deeds, at what you have done and what you have not yet done. It is much easier to keep a list of other people's mistakes than of our own, and so the teaching turns the lamp the other way.

A flower may be lovely to look at and yet have no scent, the verse observes, and so it is with fine words spoken by a person who does not act on them. A flower that is both beautiful and fragrant is like fine words that are matched by deeds, for these bear real fruit in the world. Speech, in other words, is a promise, and only when we keep it can anyone smell the flower.

From a heap of flowers, the verse says, many garlands can be made, each one different from the last. In the same way a mortal, whose time is short, should make of that time as many good deeds as he can. The picture is a cheerful one, for it suggests that goodness is not a single grand act but a pile of small blossoms, strung together one by one.

The perfume of flowers, even of sandalwood or jasmine, cannot travel against the wind, and so its reach is limited by the weather. The fragrance of a good person, however, drifts in every direction and even against the wind, because kindness is remembered long after a person has left the room. It is, the verse seems to say, the one perfume that is worth wearing.

Beside a busy highway there may lie a heap of rubbish, the verse says, and out of it a lotus may grow, sweet-smelling and delightful to the heart. In the same way, among blind and heedless crowds, the disciple of the Buddha shines out through wisdom. The image offers comfort to anyone who feels out of place: the lotus did not choose its soil, but it did choose to open, and that is the part that is ours.

The fifth chapter turns to the fool, by which it means anyone who does not learn from his own mistakes. The night is long for the sleepless, it says, and the road is long for the weary, and so the round of life is long for those who have never grasped the true teaching. Ignorance, in this telling, is not wickedness but tiredness, a weight that makes every step heavier than it needs to be.

If a traveller cannot find a companion who is wiser than himself, or at least as wise, the verse advises him to continue firmly on his own. There is no friendship to be had with a fool, it says, and a bad companion will hold a person back far more than the road itself ever could. The advice is not unkind, only honest about how strongly the company we keep shapes the people we become.

A fool is tormented, the verse says, by the thought that he has children and that he has wealth, and he worries about them day and night. Yet even the self does not belong to him in the way he imagines, so how can children or riches be his to keep? The verse does not tell us to stop loving our families or working for a living; it asks only that we hold them with open hands.

A fool who knows that he is a fool, the Dhammapada says, is for that reason wise, because the first step toward learning is to admit that there is something to learn. The fool who believes himself to be wise, on the other hand, deserves to be called a fool indeed. Pride is the one thing that closes every door, and humility is the key that opens them again.

Even if a fool spends his whole life in the company of a wise person, the verse says, he will understand nothing of the teaching, just as a spoon never tastes the soup it stirs. A person of understanding, by contrast, needs only a moment beside the wise to grasp what is being said, as the tongue knows the flavour of the soup at once. Learning, we are reminded, depends less on who stands near us than on how open we are.

Foolish people go through life as their own worst enemies, the verse says, doing wrong and then eating the bitter fruit it brings. A deed is poorly done, it explains, if we regret it afterwards, and if its result makes us weep with a tearful face. A deed is well done if it brings no regret and if we can enjoy its result with gladness, which gives each of us a simple test to apply before we act.

As long as its result has not ripened, the verse says, a fool thinks that wrongdoing is as sweet as honey. When it does ripen he comes to grief, for an evil deed does not turn sour at once like fresh milk, but follows the fool in secret, like a fire that smoulders under a covering of ashes. That is why the harm of a careless act can seem to be absent for so long, and why the teaching asks us to look at the end of a deed before we begin.

The fool longs for a reputation that he has not earned, for the first place among his fellows and for honour in every house he enters. He wishes everyone to believe that every good piece of work was done by him alone, the verse says, and in this way his desire and his pride keep growing. Cleverness gained by such a person does him no good, for it only feeds the very thing that harms him.

One road, the verse says, leads to gain, and another leads to Nibbana, and they are not the same road. Knowing this, the disciple of the Buddha should not take delight in honour or praise, but should cultivate seclusion and the quiet of his own mind. It is a closing thought for the chapter on the fool, for it shows that the greatest folly is to take the first road while hoping to arrive at the second.

The chapter on the wise begins with an unusual image: someone who points out your faults, it says, is like a person who shows you where a hidden treasure lies. Follow such a person, the verse urges, for it will go better and never worse for anyone who does so. Few of us enjoy being corrected, yet the one who corrects us kindly is giving us something that flattery never could.

Let the wise person advise and instruct, the verse says, and let him hold others back from what is wrong, for he will be dear to the good and unwelcome to the bad. For this reason, do not keep the company of bad friends, nor of the lowest kind of people, but choose good friends and the best of people. Whoever we spend our days with slowly lends us his habits, and so this advice is really about the person we want to become.

The one who drinks in the teaching, the verse says, lives happily and with a mind that is serene, for the teaching works on him as clear water works on a thirsty person. The wise take constant delight in the Dhamma taught by the noble ones, and they do not tire of hearing it again. It is the picture of a student for whom learning is no longer a duty but a pleasure that the heart asks for by itself.

Farmers lead water to their fields, arrow makers straighten their shafts and carpenters shape their wood, the verse says, but the wise tame themselves. Tradition links it to a young novice named Pandita, who is said to have watched such workers on his daily walk for food. He thought that if people can shape water and wood, he could shape his own mind, and he went back to his seat and practised until the lesson was part of him.

As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, so the wise are not moved by praise or by blame, however loudly either one is spoken. They have learned that the opinions of others pass like weather, and that peace depends on something steadier than applause. Such calm is not coldness; it is the freedom of someone who no longer needs to be told who he is.

When the wise have listened to the teachings, the verse says, their minds become tranquil like a deep lake that is clear and undisturbed. Water that is stirred up shows only mud, but water that is left alone reveals every stone at the bottom. In the same way, a quiet mind sees its own situation plainly, and nothing in it has to be hidden or feared.

The good let go of their hold on things, the verse says, and they do not chatter about the pleasures they long for. When happiness touches them or sorrow does, the wise show neither wild joy nor deep despair, and they would never seek wealth or power by unfair means, whether for themselves or for anyone else. Their steadiness comes from knowing that both joy and sorrow arrive and leave like guests, and that a good host treats each one with the same courtesy.

Among all human beings, the verse says, only a few reach the farther shore of the river of life, while the rest only run up and down the near bank. They are busy and often tired, and the days of their running are not days of crossing. The image asks us gently to look at our own busyness and to ask whether it is taking us anywhere, or only along the water's edge.

Those who follow the well-taught path, the verses say, cross over the realm of death, which is so hard to cross. The wise leave the dark way behind and take the bright one, find delight in solitude where others find little, and cleanse the mind of everything that clouds it. Those whose minds are well trained in the qualities that lead to awakening, who take joy in not clinging and whose stains are gone, shine with a light of their own and find peace in this very life.

The seventh chapter describes the arahant, the worthy one who has travelled the whole path to its end and is free from sorrow in every direction. For such a person, the verse says, the fever of the heart has gone, and the chains that once held him have fallen away. It is a portrait of complete freedom, offered less as a prize that is out of reach than as a direction in which every reader may begin to walk.

The mindful exert themselves, the verse says, and they take no pleasure in any particular dwelling, for no home holds them. Like swans that rise from a lake and leave it behind, they go from place to place with no sorrow at leaving and no desire to return. The image suits a mind that has learned to use the world without being tied to it, as a guest uses a room without mistaking it for his own.

For those who store up nothing and who know moderation in food, the verse says, the path is as hard to trace as the path of a bird in the sky. No footprint remains where a bird has flown, and so the free person leaves behind no trail of greed or resentment for anyone to follow. It is a high and quiet picture of a life that takes nothing with it and leaves nothing that needs to be undone.

The senses can be like horses, and the person who has tamed them as a skilful charioteer tames his team is calm and free from pride. Such a person has no stain left in the mind, the verse says, and even the gods look at him with admiration. There is a long journey behind that calm, but the verse suggests that the one who reaches it does not boast of it, since he no longer needs to be seen.

Such a person is patient like the earth, which does not resent those who tread upon it, and steady like a firm pillar that no storm can shift. He is also like a lake from which all the mud has settled, clear to the bottom and calm on the surface. For one who lives in this way, the verse concludes, there are no more restless wanderings, because there is nowhere left he needs to run.

Calm is the thought, calm is the word and calm is the deed of the one who is freed by right understanding and made peaceful in every part. Wherever such people live, in a village or a forest, in a valley or on a hill, that place is delightful. Forests too can be delightful, the verse adds, where ordinary people find no pleasure, for those without craving are happy there, having no wish to chase pleasures.

The eighth chapter, called Thousands, sets large numbers against small ones in order to show that what matters is quality and not quantity. Better than a thousand empty words, it says, is a single word of meaning that brings peace to the one who hears it. Anyone who has been comforted by a short and honest sentence in a time of need will understand why this verse has lasted so long.

Even if a man were to defeat a thousand times a thousand men in battle, the verse says, the one who conquers only himself is the greatest of all conquerors. Armies can be beaten and cities taken, but the habits of one's own heart are a much harder country to win. It is a surprising kind of heroism, one that is fought alone, in silence, and without any audience at all.

A person might make a thousand offerings every month for a hundred years, the verse says, seeking merit by each one. Yet a single moment of honest respect for someone who has trained himself is better than all of that giving. The lesson is not that generosity is poor, but that the heart behind a gift matters far more than its price.

For the person who is respectful by nature and who always honours his elders, four things increase, the verse says: life, beauty, happiness and strength. Whatever the exact meaning of these gifts, the verse suggests that courtesy is never wasted, since it builds trust, brings friendships and helps a person grow into the kind of elder others will wish to honour in turn. It is advice that parents in almost every land have given their children, and it is no less true for being so familiar.

Better than a hundred years lived without virtue and without self-control, the verse says, is a single day lived well and in meditation. In the same way, one day of wisdom and quiet thought is better than a hundred years of foolishness and distraction. The comparison is not about the clock but about depth, for a day in which we are fully awake can hold more life than a long stretch spent half asleep.

Better than a hundred years lived lazily and without strength of will, the verse says, is one day lived with firm and steady effort. Most of us know both kinds of day, the one that drifts by and leaves nothing behind, and the one in which we have put our whole heart to something and gone to sleep content. The Dhammapada asks us only to notice which of the two we would choose, and then to choose it.

Better than a hundred years lived without seeing how things arise and pass away, the verse says, is a single day lived in clear sight of it. Everything we know, from a mood to a mountain, is like a wave that rises, falls and is followed by another. To see this clearly is not to grow cold toward the world but to hold it more lightly and to love it with fewer fears.

Tradition links this verse, about the deathless state, to the story of Kisa Gotami, a young mother whose baby had died and who carried it from door to door asking for medicine. The Buddha told her to bring a mustard seed from any house where no one had ever died, and as she went from home to home she learned that every family had lost someone. Her grief did not vanish at once, but it became a shared sorrow rather than a lonely one, and the story says that she then asked to follow the teaching.

The last verse of the chapter makes its final comparison: better than a hundred years lived without seeing the highest teaching is one day lived in sight of it. After all the thousands and hundreds that came before it, the chapter closes on the number one, as though to say that a single clear day can outweigh a whole shelf of calendars. Quality, once again, is set above quantity, and the reader is left to wonder what a day of seeing might look like.

Make haste to do good, the ninth chapter urges, and hold your mind back from evil, for the mind that is slow to act kindly soon starts to take pleasure in wrongdoing. Good intentions that are put off until tomorrow tend to fade by the evening, while an unkind impulse needs no encouragement at all. The remedy offered here is simple: act on the good thought at once, before it has time to cool.

If a person has done wrong, the verse says, he should not do it again and again, nor set his heart upon it, for the gathering of wrong deeds is painful. If he has done good, on the other hand, he should do it again and again and set his heart upon it, for the gathering of good deeds is happiness. In this way a single act becomes a habit, and a habit, as everyone knows, slowly becomes the person who has it.

Even a wrongdoer may meet with good fortune for a while, the verse says, as long as his wrong deed has not yet ripened, and only when it ripens does he see the harm he has done. In the same way, even a good person may meet with hardship until his good deed bears fruit, and only then does he see the good he has done. The verses do not promise that the world is fair in a day, but they ask for patience and for trust in the slow work of cause and effect.

Do not think lightly of wrongdoing, the verse warns, by telling yourself that it will never come back to you, for even a water jar is filled drop by drop. In the same way, a fool is filled with evil a little at a time, and the following verse says that the wise are filled with goodness just as gradually. Small deeds repeated every day, in other words, are the true builders of character.

A merchant who travels with a small escort and a great deal of wealth avoids a dangerous road, the verse says, and a person who loves life avoids poison. In the same way we should avoid evil deeds, which are a danger far greater than any bandit. Poison cannot enter a hand that has no wound, and likewise evil cannot touch the person who does none.

Whoever harms a person who is pure and innocent, the verse says, will find that the wrong comes back upon the fool himself, like fine dust thrown against the wind. Anyone who has tried to throw dust into a strong breeze knows that most of it returns to the thrower's own face. The teaching is plain about where the real danger of cruelty lies, which is not outside us but in what it does to the one who commits it.

Not in the sky, the verse says, nor in the middle of the sea, nor in a cleft of the mountains is there any place on earth where a person can escape the result of an evil deed. It is a stern thought, but it holds a kind of mercy too, for it tells us that our deeds are never lost and that every good act, however small, is just as certain to bear fruit. Wherever we go, we carry our actions with us, and so the wisest course is to make them the kind we are glad to carry.

Everyone trembles before violence and everyone fears death, says the tenth chapter, and life is dear to all. A person who truly sees himself in other beings, it concludes, will neither strike nor cause another to strike. The rule is as old as it is simple, and it asks for nothing more than an honest effort of the imagination.

Every living being wants to be happy, the verse says, and whoever seeks his own happiness by harming other beings who want the same thing will not find it in the end. Whoever seeks happiness while harming no one, on the other hand, will find it, because his happiness takes nothing from anyone else. It is a simple piece of arithmetic in which the joy of one is never bought at the cost of another, and it is a strong argument for kindness.

Do not speak harshly to anyone, the verse says, for those you speak to will answer you in the same way. Angry speech is painful, and its echo comes back to strike the one who sent it. Every shout, we might say, is thrown against a mountain, and the mountain always has a reply.

If you can make yourself as still as a gong that has been broken and no longer rings, the verse says, then you have already come to Nibbana. No agitation is to be found in a person like that, and no quarrel can take hold of him, for a quarrel needs two voices to keep it ringing. The image turns silence into a form of strength, since the one who does not answer an insult leaves it with nowhere to go.

As a cowherd with his staff drives his cattle toward the pasture, the verse says, so old age and death drive the lives of all beings before them. The picture is not cruel, for the cowherd means his cows no harm, and the road ahead is simply the one that every living thing must take. Knowing the road, a sensible person spends the hours of the walk wisely, and does not waste them on quarrels or on grasping.

Neither going without clothes, nor matted hair, nor dirt, nor fasting, nor lying on the bare ground, nor covering oneself in ashes can purify a mortal who has not overcome doubt, the verse says. Even a person in fine clothes, however, is a true brahmin and a true monk if he is calm, tranquil and restrained, and has laid down violence toward every living being. The teaching places the sign of holiness in the manner of the heart and not in the look of the body.

Is there anyone in the world, the verse asks, who is so held back by a sense of shame that he avoids blame as a good horse avoids the whip? A fine horse needs only the lightest touch to spring forward, and a person should be like it, eager and spiritually moved by the first hint of what is wrong. With faith, virtue, effort, concentration and understanding, mindful of what he does, he will overcome this great suffering.

Why is there laughter, the eleventh chapter asks, and why is there joy, when the world is always burning with the fires of wanting? Wrapped in darkness as we are, it continues, why do we not look for a lamp? The question is asked without scorn, for it is not against laughter but against a laughter that keeps us from looking at the way things really are.

Look at this decorated body, the verse says, which people paint and care for and fill with plans, though it is often ill and has no lasting hold on anything. It wears out, it is a home for many illnesses and it breaks up in the end, because life ends in death. The thought is not cruel but practical, for a person who sees how fragile the body is will spend less of his life in worry over its looks and more in the care of the mind.

The body is like a city, the verse says, built of bones and plastered over with flesh and skin, and stored inside it are ageing, death, pride and deceit. It is a blunt description, yet it is offered with calm and without disgust, as an architect might describe the weak points of a building he cares about. Knowing what the house is made of, we can look after it kindly and still refuse to be ruled by it.

Even the splendid chariots of kings wear out in time, the eleventh chapter observes, and the body too must grow old. The teaching of the good, however, does not grow old, for the wise pass it from one to another across the years. The verse speaks of age without fear and offers a quiet consolation: what we love and understand can outlast the body that carried it.

The person of little learning grows old like an ox, the verse says, for his body grows larger while his wisdom grows not at all. The remark is aimed at those who let the years pass without asking what they mean, and it is kinder than it sounds, because the cure is always close at hand. A person who begins to learn today, at any age, has already started to grow in the better direction.

Tradition says that these words came from the Buddha at the moment of his awakening, after a long search through many lives for the builder of the house. Now you are seen, house-builder, he is said to have declared, and you will not build a house for me again, for all the rafters are broken and the ridgepole is shattered. The builder is craving and the house is the body with its round of rebirth, and the verse sounds like a long breath of relief at the end of a long task.

Those who did not live wisely in their youth, and who gathered neither wealth nor wisdom, sit in old age like worn-out herons beside a pond that has no fish, the verse says. They lie about like bows that have been broken, sighing over the days that are gone and cannot be called back. The verses are not meant to shame the old, but to remind the young that youth is a store of strength which is best spent while it lasts.

If a person holds himself dear, the twelfth chapter says, he should guard himself well, as a watchman guards a house through the long hours of the night. He should first establish himself in what is right, and only then teach others, and in this way the wise avoid pain and reproach. A teacher whose own life does not agree with his words is like a lamp that gives no light, and no one can find his way by it.

As a person instructs others, the verse says, so should he act himself, for only a person who has tamed himself well can help others to be tamed. The verse admits that this is difficult, for the self is the hardest of all things to tame. The teacher who knows how hard the work is, because he has been doing it, is the one whose advice a student is most likely to trust.

Oneself is one's own refuge, the verse says, for who else could it be? When a person has trained himself well, he gains a refuge that is hard to find anywhere else in the world. Friends and teachers can show us the door, but the shelter we walk into is the one that we have built in our own minds.

The wrong that a person does is born from himself, the verse says, and it is made by himself, and it grinds the fool down as a diamond cuts through a stone. A person who has no virtue at all is like a creeper that strangles the tree on which it grows, for he does to himself exactly what his enemy would wish. Bad deeds and deeds that harm ourselves are easy to do, it adds, while good deeds that help us are very hard to do.

It is by oneself that wrong is done, the verse says, and by oneself that a person is made unclean. It is likewise by oneself that wrong is left undone and one is made pure, for purity and impurity belong to each person alone. No one, however loving or learned, can purify another, and that is why the work must always begin at home.

However great the needs of others may be, the verse says, do not neglect your own true welfare. Having understood what that welfare is, a person should be intent upon the highest goal. The advice is not selfish, for a person who has no peace of his own has little to offer anyone else, and the best help is given from a steady place.

The thirteenth chapter, which is called The World, opens with a call like the sound of a bell in the early morning. Rise up and do not be careless, it says, but follow the good path with all your heart, for whoever walks it lives happily both in this world and in the next. The verse does not frighten the reader; it only invites him to wake, as one wakes on a bright morning, and to begin.

Look upon the world as you would look upon a bubble or a mirage, the verse advises, and the king of death will not see you. Come and look at this world, the next verse invites, as at a painted royal chariot, in which fools sink down while the wise cling to nothing. The image is not meant to make life seem worthless, but to loosen the grip of the person who clutches at everything as if it were permanent.

Tradition links this verse to Angulimala, a robber who was feared throughout the countryside until he met the Buddha, gave up violence and became a monk. A person who was careless before and is careful afterwards, the verse says, lights up this world like the moon when it comes free from a cloud. The next verse widens the promise, for whoever covers an evil deed with a good one shines in the same way, which means that no past is so dark that a clear light cannot rise from it.

This world is blind, the verse says, and only a few in it can see clearly. Like a bird that has slipped free of the hunter's net, only a few rise up into the open sky of a happier state. The verse is not a judgment on others but a description of how easy it is to be caught in the web of habit without even noticing the strands.

Swans travel along the path of the sun, the verse says, and in the tradition those with great powers of mind are said to travel through the air. In the same way, the wise are led out of the world, having conquered Mara and all of his army. The picture is a bright one, of a long and graceful flight at the end of a hard struggle, and it shows how the book likes to pair effort with ease.

A person who tells lies and scoffs at everything beyond the present moment, the verse says, will find that there is no evil he is unwilling to do. Misers, it adds, do not praise giving, and fools find no joy in generosity, while the wise delight in giving and are made happy by it. Honesty and open-handedness are shown here as two sides of one character, and the lack of both as the beginning of a long downhill road.

Better than ruling over the entire earth, the verse says, better than going to a heavenly world, and better than being lord of all the worlds is the fruit of stream-entry, the first great step on the path. The one who has entered the stream has joined a current that flows toward freedom, and tradition says that such a person does not fall away. The chapter closes on a note of quiet confidence, for it values the inner gain over every kind of outer power.

The fourteenth chapter praises the Awakened One as a person whose victory can never be undone and whom nothing in the world can follow, because his range is without limit. No craving remains in him, no net of desire that could catch him and drag him anywhere, and so, the verses ask, by what path could anyone lead him astray? The questions leave us amazed, for they describe a freedom so complete that there is nothing in it left to hold.

The wise are intent on meditation, the verse says, and they take delight in the peace that comes of putting worldly things aside. Even the gods hold dear those who are awake and mindful, it adds, as if the whole of creation leaned toward people who live with attention. The quiet life described here is not an escape from the world, since it is the ground from which a person's kindness toward the world can grow.

Four things are difficult, the chapter says: to be born as a human being, to live out the life of a mortal, to hear the true teaching, and for an awakened one to appear in the world. The list is meant to make us feel how rare and precious this present chance is, rather than to make us anxious. If you are alive and listening to the teaching, then you already hold a gift that is far from common.

In the chapter called The Buddha, one verse is often described as a summary of the whole teaching in a single breath. Avoid all evil, it says, do what is good, and cleanse your own mind, and this is what the awakened ones have taught. A later verse fills in the details of daily life, which are not to despise or harm others, to keep within the rules, to eat in moderation, to live in quiet places and to give yourself to meditation.

Patience that bears things without anger is the highest of all disciplines, the verse says, and Nibbana is the highest of all goals, as the awakened ones declare. A person who harms others cannot be called a true monk, it adds, and one who hurts others is not a true seeker of peace. The test of a holy life is thus not what is worn or recited but what is done to the people nearby, and the first part of that test is how we bear their faults.

Not even a rain of gold coins, the verse says, could satisfy the hunger of our desires, which have so little flavour and bring so much pain. The wise know this, and so, even where the pleasures are heavenly, they take no delight in them, but find their joy in the ending of craving. It is easy to nod at such a verse and difficult to live by it, for each of us has some wish that we are certain, this time, will be the last.

Driven by fear, the verses say, many people go for shelter to hills, forests, groves and sacred trees, but none of these places can give shelter from the sorrows of the mind. A safer refuge, the chapter says, is the Buddha, the teaching and the community of monks, seen with understanding of the Four Noble Truths. These truths are suffering, its origin, its ending and the Eightfold Path that leads to that ending, and a refuge built on them can be carried anywhere.

A person of such greatness is hard to find, the verse says, and he is not born everywhere, but the family in which such a wise one is born is made happy. Blessed is the birth of Buddhas, it says, and blessed is the teaching of the true Dhamma, and blessed is the harmony of the community, for those who practise together strengthen one another. The verses count their blessings with a few plain words, and the reader is invited to count them too.

Whoever honours those who are worthy of honour, the verse says, whether they are Buddhas or their disciples, who have overcome all obstacles and crossed beyond sorrow and lamentation, gains a merit that no one can measure. It is a reminder that respect is not a small thing, since it turns the heart toward what is good and keeps it from turning toward what is merely loud. The chapter on the Buddha ends with this bow, a gesture of gratitude toward everyone who has found the way and shown it to others.

The fifteenth chapter is called Happiness, and it begins by describing how happily we may live without hatred, even among people who hate. We may live free of sickness among the sick, the verse continues, and free of anxiety among the anxious, as long as we do not let their state become ours. It is a picture of happiness that does not wait for the world around us to improve.

Happily we live, the verse says, those of us who own nothing, and we shall feed on joy like the shining gods. It is not a call to poverty so much as a reminder that a person who needs little is hard to rob, since no thief can take the contentment of a mind that asks for nothing more. The lightness of such a heart is a treasure that no storeroom can hold.

Victory breeds hatred, the verse says, and the defeated lie down in pain, so that even a fair win leaves a quarrel behind it. The peaceful person lives happily, for he has set aside both victory and defeat and has no further need of either. A great deal of unhappiness comes from counting the score, and this verse suggests that we are free to put down the pencil.

There is no fire like lust, the verses say, no crime like hatred, no suffering like the clinging of body and mind, and no happiness higher than peace. Hunger is the worst of illnesses, they add, and it may be that the bodily hunger and the hunger of the heart are both meant, for neither is ever fully fed by what we give it. A person who understands this as it really is, the verse concludes, knows Nibbana as the highest happiness.

Health is the greatest of gifts, the verse says, and contentment is the greatest of riches, for a person who has enough lacks nothing. A trusted friend is the best of relatives, and Nibbana, the freedom of a mind at peace, is the highest happiness there is. The list is a quiet challenge to the usual order of things, since most of us spend our best years chasing items that are placed far lower.

Having tasted the flavour of solitude, the verse says, and the flavour of peace, a person becomes free from fear and free from evil, for he drinks the joy of the teaching. The taste is described as a kind of nourishment, the thing that the hungry heart was looking for in so many other places. Anyone who has sat alone in a quiet room and found that the silence was not empty but full will know what the verse means.

It is good to see the noble, the verses say, and to live with them is always happy, while to travel with fools brings a long sorrow, as if one were walking beside an enemy. Meeting the wise is as joyful as meeting one's own family, and so a person should follow the wise, the learned, the patient and the dutiful, as the moon follows the path of the stars. The image is of one light moving steadily among others, and it suggests that wisdom is caught less from lectures than from walking in good company.

The sixteenth chapter, called Affection, begins by observing a plain fact about the heart. It is painful not to see those whom we love, the verse says, and it is just as painful to see those whom we dislike. Our peace is thus at the mercy of who walks into the room, so long as we depend wholly on likes and dislikes for it.

Because parting from the dear is painful, the verse says, a person should not hold anything too dear. Those who have nothing that they cling to as loved or unloved are bound by no chains. A mind that does not need its comforts in order to be at ease is a mind that the loss of them cannot break.

From affection grief is born, the verse says, and from affection fear is born, but for one who is wholly free of it there is no grief, and so no fear. Teachers explain that this points to clinging, a grasping love that cannot bear to lose what it holds, and not to love itself in its open and generous form. The teaching asks us to hold dear things gently, so that when they pass, they do not take our peace with them.

Tradition tells of Visakha, a wealthy and generous woman who supported the Buddha's community and who was heartbroken when her young granddaughter died. She came to the Buddha in tears, the story says, and he spoke to her of the way that grief is born from the things we hold most dear. The story does not scold her for loving, but offers the hard comfort of understanding, which is that sorrow is the shadow of affection and that wisdom can make the shadow lighter.

The one who is endowed with virtue and with insight, the verse says, who is firm in the teaching, speaks the truth and does his own duty, is dear to everyone. Affection of this kind is not clinging but the natural warmth that follows good character, in the way that a lamp is loved for its light and not for its price. The verse shows the other face of the word, that to be dear to others is a gift we earn by what we are.

When a man has been away for a long time and returns safely from afar, the verse says, his relatives, friends and well-wishers come out to welcome him. In the same way, a person who has done good is welcomed by his own good deeds when he goes from this world to the next, as loved ones greet a dear friend. It is a gentle picture of the chapter on affection coming full circle, for it shows that the only companions who truly go with us are the good things we have done.

Give up anger, says the seventeenth chapter, and let go of pride, and overcome every bond that ties you down. No suffering can fall upon the person who does not cling to mind and body as his own, and who calls nothing his possession. The two faults named here, anger and pride, are close companions, for each is the defence of a self that is afraid of being small.

Anger rises like a chariot that has begun to run away with its driver, and most of us are carried along behind it. Whoever can check it in the moment of its rising, the verse says, deserves to be called a true charioteer, while others merely hold the reins. To master the feeling at its first stirring, before it has gathered speed, is the whole of the skill.

Conquer anger by the absence of anger, says the seventeenth chapter, and conquer evil by good, for no fault is cured by feeding it. Conquer the miser with generosity, and conquer the liar with the truth, for each fault is best met by its opposite. It is a strategy of patience rather than of force, and it works because it leaves the other person with nothing to push against.

Speak the truth, the verse says, do not yield to anger, and give, even if you have only a little, for by these three a person comes into the presence of the gods. The sages who harm no one and keep the body under control, it adds, go to the deathless state, where there is no more grief. Their way is one of daily training, day and night, and for those who keep it up the stains of the mind fade away.

This is an old saying, the verses remark: people blame the one who sits silent, they blame the one who talks a great deal, and they blame the one who speaks in moderation. No one in the world escapes blame, for there never was, and there never will be, a person who is wholly blamed or wholly praised. If that is so, then the opinion of the crowd is a poor compass, and a calm person would do better to steer by his own honest sense of what is right.

Yet there is the person whom the wise praise day after day, the verse says, who is without blemish and whose conduct is guided by wisdom and virtue. Who could find fault with such a person, the verse asks, any more than with a piece of pure gold taken fresh from a river? Even the gods praise such a person, it adds, and the best sign of worth is not the loudness of praise but the wisdom of those who give it.

Guard against anger of the body, the verses say, and keep the body under control, giving up wrong conduct and practising good conduct instead. Do the same with speech, and do the same with the mind, for in each of these three doors anger may come in. The wise who are restrained in body, speech and mind are truly well restrained, and this closes the chapter on anger with a simple map of where to stand watch.

The eighteenth chapter, called Impurity, begins by addressing a person who is like a withered yellow leaf, near the end of the road, with no supplies packed for the journey. Make an island for yourself, it says, strive quickly and become wise, and when you are purified of stain you will go on to the company of the noble. It is a stern opening, yet its message is kind, for it tells us that the time to prepare is not when we are tired but when we still have light.

Little by little, moment by moment, the verse says, a wise person should remove his own impurities, as a smith removes the dross from silver. Nothing is done in a day, and the metal does not become bright all at once, but each small cleaning leaves it a little purer than before. Anyone who has felt discouraged by the slowness of his own change will find that this is a comfortable and honest picture of how it goes.

The eighteenth chapter, on impurity, compares wrongdoing to rust, which is born from iron and yet slowly eats the very iron from which it came. A person's own deeds, it says, carry him toward a sorrowful end, so the harm does not come from outside but grows within the one who does wrong. The chapter names ignorance as the worst stain of all, because a mind that cannot see its own rust has no reason to clean it.

Failure to study is the stain on learning, the verse says, neglect is the stain on a home, laziness is the stain on beauty, and carelessness is the stain on a guard. Stinginess is the stain on a giver, and evil deeds are stains in this world and the next. Worse than all of these, however, is ignorance, which is the worst stain there is, and the person who removes it is free of stain for good.

Life is easy, the verse says, for the person who is shameless, bold as a crow, quick to speak ill of others and arrogant in his ways. It is hard for the modest person who always seeks purity, who is not attached to things, who does not push himself forward and who lives a clean life with clear understanding. The verse does not say that the hard road is the unhappy one, only that the easy one is not the one that leads where we should like to go.

Whoever destroys life, speaks falsehood, takes what has not been given or loses himself in intoxicating drink, the verse says, is digging up his own root even in this present world. Know this, good person, that such evil states are hard to restrain, and do not let greed and wickedness drag you into long suffering. The image of the root is a careful one, for it suggests that a person who acts in these ways is not only doing wrong but cutting away the ground that holds him up.

The faults of others are easily seen, the verse says, but our own are hard to see. We sift through other people's mistakes like chaff, while we hide our own as a cunning gambler hides a losing throw of the dice. The picture is a little comic, for there is something absurd in hiding what we already know, and honesty with oneself costs far less than the hiding.

The nineteenth chapter, called The Just, says that a person is not fair merely because he has decided a case, especially if he has decided it in haste. The wise person examines both what is right and what is wrong, and guards the law without favour to either side. Such a person, the verse says, is called one who stands by the teaching, and the description fits anyone who has ever had to settle a quarrel between friends.

A person is not wise merely because he speaks a great deal, the verse says, for the one who is called wise is secure in himself, free from hatred and free from fear. In the same way, a person is not a bearer of the teaching because of the words he can say, but because, having heard even a little, he lives by it. Wisdom is thus measured by what is done with words and not by how many are spoken, and a quiet person may be richer than a loud one.

A person is not an elder because his hair has turned grey, the verse says, for he may be merely ripe in years and empty of anything else. The one in whom there are truth, virtue, harmlessness, restraint and self-mastery, who is free from stain and wise, is the one who deserves to be called an elder. The verse is a gentle reproof to anyone who expects respect as a right of age, and a gentle encouragement to anyone who has earned it.

A person who is envious, selfish and deceitful does not become admirable merely by speaking beautifully or by having a pleasing face, the verse says. But one who has cut these faults out, torn them up by the root, and who is wise and free from hatred, is the one who is truly called beautiful. It is an old and consoling idea that real beauty grows from the inside outwards, and that nobody is too plain to have it.

A person who is undisciplined and speaks falsely does not become a true monk by shaving his head, the verse says, and no one who is full of desire and greed can be one. The one who always calms evil, small and great, is called a monk because of that calming, and for no other reason. The sign of a holy life is thus the quieting of harm in oneself, and a person may carry no outward sign at all and still have it.

A person is not noble because he harms living beings, the verse says, but is called noble because he is harmless toward all of them. It adds a warning that neither vows and rules, nor much learning, nor deep concentration, nor a life spent alone should lead us to believe that the highest freedom has been won. The seeker should not rest content, it concludes, until the stains of the mind have been brought to an end, and this honest restlessness is the last lesson of the chapter on the just.

The twentieth chapter, called The Path, names the best of all roads as the Noble Eightfold Path, and the best of all truths as the Four Noble Truths. Dispassion is called the best of states, and the one who sees clearly the best of human beings. This path, the verse concludes, is the only one that leads to the purifying of insight, and the reader is urged to follow it.

You yourselves must make the effort, says the twentieth chapter, for the Buddhas can only point the way. Those who enter the path and keep their minds steady in meditation will be freed from the bonds of Mara, the tempter who stands for everything that holds the heart in sleep. No teacher, however great, can walk the road in anyone's place, and this verse says so with beautiful honesty.

All made things are impermanent, the verse says, and when a person sees this with true insight, he begins to turn away from suffering. The same chapter adds that all things are without a lasting self, and that seeing this too is the road to purity. The thought is hard at first, like cold water, but those who accept it often find that the grip of worry is loosened.

The person who does not rise when it is time to rise, the verse says, who is young and strong yet idle, with a mind full of weak resolutions, will never find the way to wisdom. The warning is not about tiredness, which every person feels, but about the lazy habit of waiting for a better moment that never arrives. Strength is a loan from the years, and it is best spent while the loan lasts.

Be watchful of your speech, the verse says, be well restrained in your mind, and do nothing harmful with your body. Keep these three ways of acting clean, and you will win the path that the sages have made known. The advice is as practical as a checklist, for we always do something with our words, our thoughts and our hands, and each of the three is a place where we can choose well.

Wisdom springs from meditation, the verse says, and without meditation wisdom wanes away, as a plant dies when it is not watered. Knowing this twofold path of gain and loss, a person should so conduct himself that his wisdom may grow. It is a modest piece of advice, to set aside time for quiet thought each day, and yet the verse suggests that everything else we hope to understand depends on it.

Cut down the forest of desire, the verse says, and not only a single tree, for fear is born in the forest. As long as even the smallest undergrowth of wanting is left uncut, the mind remains in bondage, like a calf that still drinks at its mother's side. The image is a reminder that half-measures do not free us, since a single remaining root can send up the whole thicket again.

Here I shall live in the rains, here in winter and in summer, thinks the fool, and he does not see the danger that stands close behind his plans. The verse has no objection to planning, and every sensible person arranges his seasons, but it warns against the belief that the arrangements will last for ever. A home, a career and a future are all borrowed from time, and the wise person lives in them gratefully and lightly.

The flood that carries off a sleeping village returns in this chapter, for death sweeps away the person whose mind is clinging to the pleasures of the day. Sons are no protection, the verse says, nor are fathers or other relatives, and no family can stand between a person and death. Understanding this, the wise, who are held firm by good conduct, quickly clear the path that leads to Nibbana, as a traveller clears a road before the light fades.

The twenty-first chapter is a collection of miscellaneous verses, and it opens with a piece of practical wisdom. If by giving up a smaller happiness a person can see a greater happiness, the wise person will give up the smaller for the greater. A child who saves a sweet to share at a feast is doing this, and so is anyone who puts aside an easy pleasure today for a lasting good tomorrow.

A person who seeks his own happiness by bringing suffering to others, the verse says, is entangled in the bonds of hatred and is not set free from it. He has tied himself to those he has harmed, because their pain returns to him as resentment and as fear. The only way out is the opposite road, in which our gain is never bought with someone else's loss.

What should be done is left undone, the verses say, and what should not be done is done instead, and so the stains of the proud and heedless only increase. For those who are always mindful of the body and who do not do what should not be done, but do what should be done, the stains come to an end. It is a kind of housekeeping of the mind, and its first rule is that the little jobs we neglect become large ones.

Always well awake, the verses say, are the followers of Gotama, the Buddha, who day and night keep in mind the Buddha, the teaching and the community of monks. They are also mindful of the body and take delight in harmlessness and in meditation. A series of short verses repeats the same pattern, as though a morning bell were being rung six times, each time on a different thought to wake up with.

A person who has faith and virtue, who has gained a good name and a fair share of wealth, is honoured wherever he goes, the verse says. The good shine from afar like the snowy peaks of the Himalaya, while the bad cannot be seen at all, like arrows shot into the dark. The comparison is a quiet one: goodness is visible across great distances, while harm hides itself and strikes where it is not looked for.

The one who sits alone, sleeps alone and walks alone, the verse says, tireless and unwearied, and who tames himself alone, will find his delight at the edge of the forest. It is a short verse and a gentle one, for it does not ask the reader to leave home but only to find, somewhere, a place of quiet. Solitude of this kind is not loneliness, since it is a time of meeting oneself, and it is the best preparation for meeting others.

The twenty-second chapter is called Hell, and in the old teaching the word names the deep suffering that wrongdoing can bring about. A person who tells lies comes to sorrow, the first verse says, and so does the one who does wrong and then denies it, for both are held by what they have done. The chapter treats the subject as a matter of cause and effect and not as a threat, and its first lesson is that a hidden deed is still a deed.

As sharp kusa grass cuts the hand that grasps it wrongly, the verse says, so a holy life wrongly handled drags a person down into suffering. A slack effort, a broken vow or a doubtful way of life produces no great fruit, it adds, and a lax wanderer only scatters more dust. If something is to be done, the verse concludes, let it be done with all one's strength, for a half-hearted effort at something good can wound the one who makes it.

A wrong deed is better left undone, the verse says, for it torments the doer afterwards, while a good deed is better done, since nobody regrets it. Guard yourself, it continues, as people guard a border city, with watchmen both inside and out, and do not let the moment slip by. Those who let it pass will grieve over it, the verse warns, and the grief is the sorrow of what might have been done.

To be ashamed of what is not shameful, and not ashamed of what is, is a wrong view, the verses say. So is fearing what should not be feared, and feeling no fear of what should, as is seeing fault where there is none and missing it where it lies. Those who know a fault as a fault, and a harmless thing as harmless, hold the right view, and it leads them toward a good road.

The twenty-third chapter takes its name from the elephant, which in ancient times was trained to carry kings into battle and to stand firm while arrows fell around it. Just as such an elephant endures every shot, the verse says in the voice of the teacher, so shall I endure the harsh words of others, for the world is full of people who speak carelessly. The chapter adds that a tamed elephant is a fine thing, but that the person who has tamed himself is finer still.

Well-trained mules are excellent, the verse says, and so are thoroughbred horses and great elephants with their mighty tusks. Better than any of them, however, is the person who has tamed himself, for none of those animals can carry anyone to the untrodden place that a tamed self can reach. The comparison lifts a humble skill, the training of oneself, above the glitter of the finest riding animals, and it does so without any show.

Formerly this mind of mine wandered wherever it liked and as it pleased, says the teacher, but now I shall hold it firmly, as an elephant driver holds a wild elephant with his hook. Take delight in heedfulness and guard your mind, he adds, and draw yourself out of the evil way, as an elephant lifts itself out of the mud in which it has sunk. The two pictures are of control and rescue, and they remind us that taming the mind is partly a matter of holding on and partly a matter of climbing out.

If you find a wise and steady companion, the chapter says, walk with him, glad and thoughtful, and overcome every danger on the way. If you find none, then go on alone like an elephant in the great forest, or like a king who has left a conquered country behind him. There is companionship in the first case and freedom in the second, and the verse sees nothing to fear in either.

Good are friends when need arises, the verses say, and good is contentment with whatever one has, and good is the store of kind deeds that a person carries at the end of life. Good is the care of one's mother and father, and good is the respect shown to monks and holy people. The list closes with virtue that lasts into old age, with settled faith, with the gaining of wisdom and with the avoiding of all evil, a modest inventory of the things that make a life feel well spent.

The twenty-fourth chapter is about craving, which in the heedless grows like a creeping vine that wraps itself around everything it touches. Whoever is overcome by this fierce thirst finds his sorrows multiplying, the verse says, as grass grows quickly after the rain. The remedy it offers is to dig up the root, so that craving cannot rise again and again like a weed that has only been cut back.

Whoever is overcome by this fierce and clinging craving, the verse says, finds his sorrows growing as thickly as grass after a rainfall. But whoever overcomes this craving, which is so hard to overcome, finds that sorrow slips from him as water slips from a smooth leaf. The difference between the two is not the world around them but what they do with the wanting that rises inside.

Dig up the root of craving, the teacher tells his listeners, as one who needs a certain fragrant root digs up the stubborn grass around it. A tree that has been cut down will grow again if its root is firm and unharmed, and in the same way this suffering springs up again and again while the hidden craving has not been pulled out. The remedy is to go deeper than the surface, for craving that is only trimmed will return, and the work of uprooting it is done by understanding.

Those who are bound by craving, the verse says, run about like a hunted hare, held fast by the fetters that they cannot see, and they suffer again and again for a long time. The hare in the snare pulls harder as it panics, and the harder it pulls the tighter the loop becomes. Therefore, the verse concludes, the person who wishes to be free should put craving away, and so stop the pulling that tightens the rope.

The wise do not call a bond of iron, wood or hemp strong, the verse says, for these can be cut with a knife. The strongest bond is the infatuation with jewels and ornaments, and the longing for children and partners, which drags a person down and yet looks so loose that nobody notices it. Having cut even this bond, the wise go forward without longing, and they leave sensual pleasure behind.

Those who are carried away by lust, the verse says, fall back into the stream that they have made themselves, as a spider falls into the web that it has spun. The wise cut through the thread and go forward without longing, leaving all suffering behind them.
