It is a sober image of how much of our trouble we weave out of our own wanting, and also of how the same hands that wove the web can cut it.

Let go of what is behind you, the verse says, let go of what is ahead of you, and let go of what lies in the middle. Having gone to the farther shore of existence, with a mind that is released on every side, you will not come again to birth and old age. The advice is almost a travel instruction, and it is wonderfully complete, since it leaves nothing to carry in any direction of time.

The gift of the teaching surpasses every other gift, the verse says, its taste surpasses every other taste, and delight in it surpasses every other delight. The ending of craving, it adds, conquers all suffering, and it is the one victory that nobody has to take from anyone else. As weeds are the ruin of a field, so passion is the ruin of people, and for that reason a gift given to those who are free from passion yields a great harvest.

The twenty-fifth chapter, called The Monk, opens by praising restraint in each of the senses, in the eye, in the ear, in the nose and in the tongue. Restraint in body, in speech and in mind is good as well, it continues, and the one who is restrained everywhere is freed from all suffering. Restraint here does not mean closing the doors, but learning to stand at them, so that what comes in is welcomed with attention and not simply allowed to carry us away.

The one who is controlled in hand and foot and in speech, the verse says, who delights in quiet meditation and is content to be alone, is the one who is called a monk. When such a person speaks, his tongue is restrained, his words are wise and free from conceit, and he explains the meaning of the teaching in a way that is sweet to the ear. The picture joins two things that seem opposite, a deep inner quiet and a clear, generous voice, and suggests that the second grows out of the first.

One should not despise what one has received, the verse says, nor envy the gains of others, for the person who envies others does not reach a steady mind. Even a monk who receives very little, if he does not look down on it and lives honestly and with energy, is praised by the gods themselves. Contentment is thus presented as a kind of skill, the art of being fed by what is on the plate and not by what is on the next one.

The twenty-fifth chapter is addressed to the monk, the one who has left home to follow the path, but its advice is useful to anyone. Bail out the water from your boat, it says, for when it is emptied it will go lightly across the lake. If you cut off greed and hatred, the weight that slows you will be gone, and you will reach freedom with far less effort than you now imagine.

Meditate, the verse says, and do not be careless, and do not let your mind whirl about among sensual pleasures, so that you will not cry out in pain afterwards. There is no meditation for one who has no wisdom, it adds, and no wisdom for one who does not meditate, and the person who has both is close to Nibbana. The two are like a pair of wings, since a bird with only one of them will turn in circles, and with both it can fly.

The monk who has entered an empty place and whose mind is at peace, the verse says, who sees the teaching rightly, feels a delight that is beyond the ordinary human kind. Whenever he understands the rise and fall of body and mind, he gains joy and happiness, and for those who know it, this is called the deathless. The empty place may be a hut or a quiet corner or only a pause in a busy day, and the delight comes not from the place but from the clarity that the quiet allows.

As the jasmine plant lets its withered flowers fall, the verse says, so should you let go of lust and of hatred, completely and for good. The plant does not struggle to get rid of the old blossoms, for they simply drop when their time has come, and the freshness that follows is never in doubt. Letting go is described here not as a loss but as a natural part of growth.

Reprove yourself by yourself, says the verse, and examine yourself by yourself, and so, guarded and mindful, you will live happily. For oneself is the protector of oneself, and oneself is the refuge of oneself, and therefore you should look after yourself as a merchant looks after a fine horse. It is a closing reminder that the teacher's work in the end gives way to the student's own, and that the best guardian anyone has is a mind that has learned to watch itself kindly.

The twenty-sixth and last chapter is called The Brahmin, a word that in this book means a truly noble person, and it begins with a call to cut off the stream of craving. Strive, it says, and push away your sensual desires, and when you know the ending of all made things you will know what is not made. The person for whom there is neither the near shore nor the far shore, who is fearless and free from every bond, is the one the verse calls noble.

The sun shines by day, says the verse, and the moon lights up the night, and the warrior shines in his armour. The noble person shines in meditation, but the Buddha shines through the day and through the night with the radiance of his own mind. Each kind of light belongs to its own time and place, the verse seems to say, while the light of an awakened mind needs no hour and no fuel.

Because he has driven out evil he is called a brahmin, the verse says, and because he has sent away his own impurities he is called one who has gone forth. A later verse names the same person as the one who does no evil by body, by speech or by mind, and who is restrained in all three of these doors. The names are only names, and the book keeps returning to the same simple test of what a person is doing with his hands, his words and his thoughts.

One does not become noble by matted hair, by family or by birth, the verse says, but by truth and righteousness. In the one who has them there is blessedness, and that person is the true brahmin. In this way the teaching places worth in conduct rather than rank, and it draws a portrait of a man who is free in the heart, not merely in name.

What is the use of matted hair, the verse asks, and what is the use of a cloak of antelope skin, when the tangle is within and only the outside is being cleaned? The question is put to the person who looks the part but has not looked inside. It is a friendly reminder that the work of becoming noble is done in the place where nobody else can see it, and that no costume, however humble, will do it for us.

The person who wears robes made of rags, who is lean from effort and who meditates alone in the forest, is called noble by the verse. It does not call a person noble because of his origin or his mother's womb, and it remarks that one who has many possessions is merely called sir. The one who owns nothing and clings to nothing, it says, is the person who is truly noble, and no title can add to that.

The one who endures abuse, beating and imprisonment without anger, the verse says, and whose strength and whose army is patience, is the one it calls noble. It is a strange kind of power, since it is shown by what a person does not do when he has every excuse to do it. It recalls the elephant in battle from an earlier chapter, and the book seems to come round to its own earlier picture.

One who has laid down violence toward all beings, whether weak or strong, and who neither kills nor causes others to kill, is the one the verse calls noble. Such a person is friendly among the hostile, peaceful among the violent and unattached among those who cling. It is the first chapter's lesson turned into a person, for that chapter said that hatred ends only by love, and here is someone in whom it has.

One who speaks words that are gentle, instructive and true, so that nobody is offended by them, is called noble in this chapter. He takes nothing in the world that has not been given to him, whether long or short, small or large, fair or foul. The two lines go together, for honest speech and honest hands are the outer signs of a mind that has no need to deceive or to grab.

One who has gone beyond clinging to both good and evil, the verse says, and who is without sorrow and without stain, is pure. Such a person is spotless like the moon, serene and undisturbed, with no more delight in the cycle of becoming. The moon appeared before, freed from a cloud, and here it returns as a whole and quiet light, without any cloud left to pass.

The one who has passed beyond this muddy, dangerous and difficult road of delusion, the verse says, who has crossed over to the other shore, is meditative and steady, free from doubt and free from clinging. Such a person has given up sensual pleasures and wanders without a home, and for him the long road that began so many verses ago has come to firm and dry ground. In the first verse the wheel followed the ox, and here at last is a walker who has put the cart down.

One who knows, even in this very life, the end of his own suffering, the verse says, has put down the burden and is free from every bond. Having done everything that was to be done, such a person has nothing further to prove and nothing further to carry, and the effort of all the earlier chapters finds its rest. Many readers will take from this verse a small piece of relief, that the heaviest loads are the ones we have picked up and can set down.

In its closing verses the Dhammapada describes the one who clings to no pleasure, like a drop of water that rolls from a lotus leaf, or a mustard seed that slips from the point of a needle. Such a person moves through the world without fear, anger or grasping, and lust, hatred, pride and deceit have fallen away from him. The book ends where it began, with the mind, and leaves each reader to walk the path in his own way and at his own pace.
